name: Coffee shop
tagline: Espresso, pastries and 18 seats on a real New York block: real rent, real permits, real inspectors.

unit.name: order
unit.note: Planning assumption from research notes (economics.md, 2026 planning model): an average ticket of $8.50 before sales tax (a drink, sometimes with a pastry). Menu anchors seen by the note's author in 2026: latte $4.25-$6.99, croissant $4.00-$5.49. Ingredients, food and spoilage are 26% of sales = $2.21 per order; cups, lids and napkins (another 2%) are a separate monthly cost line, so the full cost of goods is 28%. No public statistic of the average NYC cafe ticket exists (searched November 14, 2026). Input prices behind the cost line were checked: retail ground coffee $9.25 per lb and whole milk $4.10 per gallon in October 2026 (BLS via FRED), a 12 oz hot cup 4.6 cents (WebstaurantStore, $45.99 per 1,000).

market.note: D06 revision. (1) unitsPerSlotMonth stays 6,000 (200 orders a day): still a planning point, not a statistic. Cross-checks found: Joe Coffee, an ordering app for independent shops, reports an average ticket of $8.47 across its shops (was $7.82 a year earlier; its method is not stated), which matches the pack's $8.50; BizBuySell's median coffee shop sold in the US takes $375,000 a year = $1,027 a day = about 121 orders a day at that ticket, so 200 a day is a good New York block, not the national middle. (2) priceElasticity stays -1.3 and now has an anchor: Starbucks North America, second quarter of fiscal 2025, transactions fell 4% while prices rose about 3% (-4 / 3 = -1.3). Range: -1.0 (USDA ERS report ERR-139, Okrent and Alston: own-price elasticity of all food away from home -1.02, limited service less elastic than full service) to -2.5 (Starbucks US, fourth quarter of fiscal 2024: ticket +4%, transactions -10%, a quarter with other troubles mixed in). (3) weights: reputation cut from 0.20 to 0.09, the other three keep their old ratios to each other (35 : 25 : 20). Reason: Luca (Harvard Business School working paper 12-016) measured +5-9% revenue per Yelp star for independent restaurants. In the engine one star = 0.25 of the 0-1 reputation scale, and the demand change is |elasticity| x (reputation weight / price weight) x 0.25 x (1 - own share). Old weights: 1.3 x (0.20 / 0.35) x 0.25 x 0.9 = 16.7% per star, twice the top of the measured range. New weights: 1.3 x (0.09 / 0.40) x 0.25 x 0.9 = 6.6% per star. The letter grade and word of mouth act on top of this through events and mechanics (extra.mechanics: star_rating, letter_grade_demand). Toast's 2025 survey of 650 US coffee drinkers supports keeping quality close to price: taste 53%, price 20%, convenience 17%, atmosphere 8% as the main reason to pick one shop over another (stated, not measured). All numbers were read in search results; the pages themselves could not be opened from this session.

capacity.note: Existing throughput, staff floor and ceiling are retained as unverified design assumptions. Certified supervisory coverage is required during receiving/preparation and public operation; the source does not impose a universal two-person minimum. Measure work coverage, breaks and actual throughput before calibration.

sizing.note: Revised by D02. sqftPerUnit 18 -> 21: the engine divides 60% of the floor by this number, and 18 put 26 seats into 800 sq ft, above the research notes' own 15-25. Floor budget for 800 sq ft (extra.floorPlan): service bar 120, queue and pickup 70, accessible restroom 60, back of house 120, entry 25 = 395 sq ft that never holds a chair; 405 sq ft is left for seating; at 18 net sq ft per seat that is 22 seats, and 480 / 22 = 21. Anchors: the 2022 NYC Building Code counts 15 net sq ft per person at tables and chairs, 5 net sq ft per standing person and 200 gross sq ft per person in a commercial kitchen (Table 1004.1.3, read in the city's own PDF); vendor seating charts give 11-14 sq ft per seat for fast food, 12-15 full service, 18-20 fine dining; a Russian planning guide gives 1.6 sq m (17 sq ft) per guest. unitsServedPerSizeMonth stays 170, now with a derivation: 12 open hours, mean seat occupancy 47%, mean stay 60 minutes (70% short stays of 35 minutes, 30% laptop stays of 120 minutes) = 5.6 seated orders per seat a day. Stay lengths: Bloom Intelligence Wi-Fi data, 25 US coffee shops, June-September 2026: 32 minutes for a one-time visitor, almost two hours for the most frequent ones. takeawayShare stays 0.6: no public to-go split exists for independent cafes; the National Restaurant Association puts off-premises at nearly 75% of all restaurant traffic, drive-thru included. crowdPenaltyAbove 0.9 -> 0.85: solo guests hold two-tops, so a room is full when well under all chairs are taken (see extra.mechanics effective_seats_and_table_mix). emptyPenaltyBelow 0.4 -> 0.3: evidence that an empty room repels coffee buyers is weak (one 2025 survey study on crowding as social proof), so the penalty should start later. Both thresholds stay game-balance values.

setup.name: Two-group espresso machine
Espresso grinder (Mahlkonig E65W)
Water filtration for the espresso machine
setup.note: Research notes allowance for a filter head, cartridge and fittings; listed there: Everpure ESO7 cartridge $192.94, QL2 head $41.94. Cartridges are replaced several times a year (in the maintenance line). D03 correction: cartridge life is set by gallons and hardness, not by the calendar. Pentair's spec sheet rates the Everpure ESO 7 at 5,300 grains: 600 gallons at 150 ppm, at no more than 0.5 gallons a minute, replaced when the volume is reached or at least once a year. New York City water averages about 1.8 grains per gallon (DEP), so one cartridge treats about 2,900 gallons; where Croton water is blended in, hardness can reach 7 grains and the same cartridge lasts about 760 gallons. At roughly 20 gallons a day through the espresso machine and brewer (my assumption) that is about 5 months on soft water and 5-6 weeks on the hardest.

setup.name: Customer restroom upgrade (needed for 20 or more seats)
setup.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
setup.note: Same id as in the pack; the price stays the earlier allowance (no public NYC price was found), the rule is now exact and was read in the Health Code itself. Section 81.22(b): food service establishments with a seating capacity of 20 or more shall provide toilet facilities for patrons, except premises where a permitted food service establishment operated on or before December 5, 1977; such premises must add patron toilets when a renovation needs a Department of Buildings construction permit. 81.22(d): patrons and staff may share a toilet unless patrons would have to walk through a kitchen, food preparation or storage area or utensil washing area. NYC Health counts indoor and outdoor seats together. The Plumbing Code (403.2, 403.3) adds a second step that bites when a space is built or altered: where customers must be given a toilet and the space holds more than 30 people, staff included, separate facilities are required, which two single all-gender toilet rooms satisfy; the toilets may be one story up or down. The U.S. Access Board sets no minimum room size. A one-person toilet room must carry an all-gender sign (Local Law 79 of 2016).

setup.note: NYC Admin. setup.name: Asbestos investigation (ACP-5) before the permit
setup.agency: NYC Department of Environmental Protection (certified asbestos investigator)
setup.note: Rule seen in the DOB page extract: an ACP-5 (not an asbestos project) or other asbestos form must be submitted before a DOB permit may be issued; work in buildings built after April 1, 1987 may use the ASB4 exemption. Only a DEP-certified asbestos investigator can file it. Price is my estimate: secondary guides quote $400-$1,500 for an NYC ACP-5 survey plus $25-$150 per lab sample; $900 is the midpoint for a small storefront with a handful of samples. No official price exists. The 7 days are my estimate for scheduling, sampling and lab results.

setup.name: Landmarks permit for storefront work (historic districts only)
setup.appliesIf: address is in a historic district or the building is a landmark
setup.note: LPC storefront fact sheet (2019) seen in extract: a complete storefront application gets a staff permit within 10 business days through FasTrack, otherwise within 15 business days (about 21 calendar days); incomplete applications are returned. LPC said in April 2025 that 95% of its approvals are issued at staff level. Any exterior storefront change in a historic district (sign, awning, door, window) needs the permit, and DOB will not issue its permit without it. Proposals that go to the full Commission take months (one architect guide: 90 business days or more). Fee, LPC fees page seen in extract: a flat $95 for the first $25,000 of work plus $5 for each $1,000 above, collected through the DOB NOW filing; for a $70,000 job 95 + 45 x 5 = $320. Conflict to resolve: the opened NYC Business page on landmarked property still lists the older fee, $50 for the first $25,000 of work and $3 per $1,000 above ($185 on a $70,000 job); the Landmarks Commission's own fees page (search extract; the site refused the request) gives $95 and $5. The opened page confirms the rule: a Landmarks permit is needed before any work, and for any work that needs a Buildings permit; fees are collected at the Department of Buildings.

setup.agency: NYC Department of Buildings, borough office

setup.note: Page opened (NYC311 KA-02023): "Every building built after 1938 requires a Certificate of Occupancy"; "DOB provides Letters of No Objection to confirm the legal use of a building constructed before 1938. To request a Letter of No Objection, go to the DOB Borough Office where your property is located." Page opened (NYC Business): you cannot use a building until the Department gives a Certificate of Occupancy or a temporary one. For a cafe the letter has to cover an eating and drinking establishment. Wait: one architecture firm says at least one month in a clear case. No fee is stated on either page, so cost is 0 plus the expediter time already inside architect_expediter.

setup.name: Build-out contingency reserve
setup.note: 15% of a $70,000 light renovation. NYC contractors recommend a contingency of 10-15% of hard costs (another Brooklyn contractor says 5-10% is typical); change orders rushed through without a reserve carry a 15-30% premium. The research notes budget $9,500 for the same scenario. This is a reserve, not a purchase: money not eaten by the events of extra.eventCatalog (hidden conditions, change orders, failed inspections) stays in the bank.

setup.name: Sales tax on the contractor's bill (if the work is not a capital improvement)
setup.avoidableBy: lease clause that makes the improvements the landlord's property on installation, plus Form ST-124 given to the contractor
setup.note: Pages opened (NYS Tax Department): advisory opinion TSB-A-24(54)S of November 12, 2024: "as a general rule, additions or alterations to real property for or by a tenant with respect to leased premises are presumed to be temporary in nature and do not qualify as capital improvements"; the customer gives the contractor a properly completed Form ST-124 for a capital improvement. Tax Bulletin Capital Improvements: tenant work "may not qualify if the tenant's lease does not transfer ownership of the improvement to the property owner"; its example is a salon whose lease requires the premises to be returned to their original condition, so the sinks are taxable. Materials are taxed either way. Calculation (mine): 8.875% on the labor-and-markup share of the bill (assumed 60%) x $70,000 = $3,728; on the full $70,000 the tax would be $6,212.

setup.name: Con Edison security deposit for a new business account
setup.note: Page opened (Con Edison, rights of non-residential customers): "If you are a new customer, we require a deposit as a condition of service"; "The deposit may not be more than two times your average monthly bill for the previous calendar year, unless your usage varies widely", in which case not more than twice the average monthly usage for the peak season; the customer may ask for a review and may pay half the deposit initially. Calculation (mine): electricity taken as $800 of the pack's $1,100 utilities line x 2 = $1,600. Already counted inside the existing insurance_utility_deposits item ($1,500): do not charge both. D11 check (search-seen, Con Edison nonresidential rights brochure, coned.com non-res-rights-english.pdf): the deposit may not exceed twice the average monthly bill, or twice the peak-season average when use swings; it is refunded when the account closes with nothing owed. With the pack utilities line of $1,100 that caps it near $2,200, so D01 $1,600 and D09 $1,800 both fit.

setup.name: Electrical service upgrade for espresso, ice and refrigeration loads

setup.note: Weak estimate, quote-only in real life. NYC electricians advertise $3,500-$10,000 for a 100 to 200 amp panel upgrade in a home; a commercial three-phase service costs more, so the top of that range is used. Any service change needs Con Edison coordination, which adds two to six weeks (contractor guides); Con Edison's own 2021 sheet for fleet chargers says utility-side upgrades can run 6 to 24 months depending on the existing service and the requested load. setup.name: Purchase price of an operating coffee shop
excludes: sales tax on the equipment part of the price
setup.note: BizBuySell valuation benchmarks for coffee shops and cafes sold in 2021-2025, seen in extract: median price 2.00 times the seller's yearly earnings (middle half 1.50-2.55) and 0.41 times yearly revenue (0.30-0.57); median sale price in 2025 $176,500. setup.name: SBA loan upfront guaranty fee (per $100,000 borrowed)
setup.note: SBA Information Notice 5000-881797 (fees for loans approved October 1, 2026 - September 30, 2027), read through the lender association's summary because the notice text was not readable: 2% of the guaranteed portion on loans of $150,000 or less, 3% on $150,001-$700,000, 3.5% above that; 0.25% when the loan runs 12 months or less. SBA guarantees 85% of loans up to $150,000 (seen at sba.gov), and lenders pass the fee on: $100,000 x 85% x 2% = $1,700. The 0.55% yearly servicing fee may not be charged to the borrower.

setup.name: Backflow prevention device on the water line
Under-sink grease interceptor, installed
setup.note: DEP, read on the page: every business that disposes of grease should have a properly sized grease interceptor (15 RCNY 19-11); food waste grinders are not allowed in NYC commercial establishments. Price: national cost guides put an indoor under-sink unit at $500-$3,000 installed and add 30%-50% for labor in New York; $2,500 is my figure inside that band. DEP requires that only licensed plumbers install grease interceptors, and its inspectors order an undersized unit replaced. A former cafe has one; a former shop or salon does not, and the build-out price for such a space should already include it.

setup.name: Replacement air conditioner (3-5 ton unit, installed)
setup.note: Not an opening purchase when the space comes with working air conditioning: this is what replacement costs when the old unit dies. A New York City contractor price page quotes $5,000-$12,000 installed for a 3-5 ton rooftop unit (indicative only); $8,500 is the middle. A crane lift adds $1,500 or more, and rooftop work needs Buildings Department permits. ASHRAE's median service life for rooftop air conditioners is 15 years. The lease decides whether the landlord or the tenant maintains and replaces the unit that serves only this space: read the clause and ask the unit's age before signing.

setup.name: See-through roll-down security grille
setup.note: Gothamist, 2026: a bakery owner was quoted $6,000-$7,000 to replace one gate; other reports give $5,000-$20,000. Buildings Department service notice of February 17, 2026, read in full: under Local Law 75 of 2009 grilles on Group B and M storefronts had to give at least 70% visibility by July 1, 2026 (Administrative Code 28-315.7.1), landmark buildings and historic districts exempt; non-compliance is a major violation that can be cured within 90 days, and replacing a grille needs a registered design professional and a permit. Seen in search excerpts of the press and the Council record: on June 30, 2026 the City Council voted 51-0 (Int 0910-A) to drop the deadline, so the 70% rule now applies only when a grille is newly installed or replaced.

setup.name: Fabric storefront awning with the shop name
setup.note: Job costs declared on recent Buildings Department filings, read through a permit aggregator: a single storefront awning $2,000 in Sunset Park, $2,800 in the East Village, $2,600 in an Upper East Side landmark district; retractable ones run to $15,000. The awning is a permitted job. Zoning limits what it may say: lettering no taller than 12 inches, no more than 12 sq ft, name and address only (as summarized in a LISC storefront guide; the zoning text was not opened). The 8-year fabric life is a planning value.

setup.name: Seasonal entrance vestibule (storm enclosure)
setup.note: One NYC fabricator lists temporary vestibules at $4,500-$10,000 with seasonal installation and removal included (seen in a search excerpt); $4,500 is the low end for a single door. NYC311, read on the page: storm enclosures are allowed from November 15 through April 15, and the city takes complaints about ones that have no permit, stand more than 18 inches beyond the street line or are not removed after April 15. A fabricator cites a larger allowance of 25 sq ft for eating and drinking places (not checked against the Building Code). The cost returns every winter.

setup.name: Air curtain over the front door
setup.note: Cost guide: a 48-inch unheated unit with professional installation is about $1,450; the installed range for one entrance is $900-$4,000, a heated unit can double the price, and the Northeast runs 10%-25% higher. A trade magazine case (ACHR News) describes a restaurant that ended cold-draft complaints with one.

setup.name: Dining Out NYC roadway cafe license
setup.agency: NYC Department of Transportation (Dining Out NYC)

setup.name: Roadway cafe structure: barriers, platform, furniture
setup.note: Streetsblog, April 2025: a roadway setup can easily cost more than $35,000 with city fees, construction and insurance; rental companies quote about $20,000 a season; one owner spent just over $5,000 on a simple one. $20,000 is the rental-season figure used as a purchase price for a plain compliant setup. Until 2026 the structure had to be taken down and stored every winter. The program's own fee example uses a 160 sq ft roadway cafe.

setup.name: Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation (75 or more people)
setup.agency: NYC Department of Buildings; Fire Department (FDNY) annual permit
setup.note: Read at the Buildings Department and in the Fire Department's restaurant guide: a Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation is required where 75 or more people gather indoors (200 outdoors), and the Fire Department counts restaurant staff in the 75. After the certificate an annual Fire Department Place of Assembly permit follows; its fee is on a sliding scale by occupancy and re-inspections are billed at $210 an hour. The $235 ($200 filing + $35 processing) is from the Buildings guide dated 2013 and may be out of date. The 60 days are my allowance. The real cost of crossing 74 people is not this fee: a second exit, doors that swing outward, filed seating plans and certified fire safety staff.

setup.name: Temporary Place of Assembly certificate for one event
Replace one storefront glass panel
setup.note: Glazier guides (not NYC): a fixed panel of about 4 x 6 feet costs $800-$1,500 installed, a storefront window $500-$3,000 by size and glass type; $1,150 is the midpoint for one panel. Emergency board-up is extra. Used by the break-in event; most leases make the tenant responsible for the glass.

setup.name: Used two-group espresso machine (refurbished)
setup.note: A US dealer's 2026 guide puts a used two-group La Marzocco Linea Classic at $5,000-$8,000; single listings seen in search results: $4,900 used and $8,500 refurbished (2017 build), against $12,730-$16,480 new. $6,500 is the middle of the guide's range. Dealer warranties on used machines are 1-3 months of parts, against 12-13 months on a new one. 60 months of remaining life is my assumption: half of a 10-year service life. Have a technician open the boiler and look for scale before you pay.

setup.name: Upgrade to a dual-boiler specialty espresso machine
setup.note: A new two-group La Marzocco Linea Classic S was listed at $12,730 at one US retailer and $16,480 at another (search results, November 2026); the upgrade costs the difference from the $7,600 compact machine = $5,130. 144 months: the upper half of the 10-15 years a service company gives for a maintained machine. New machines carry a 13-month parts and labor warranty that requires installation by a factory-certified technician and water treatment. The quality bonus is a game value.

setup.name: Used milk fridge and reach-in refrigerator
setup.note: Dealer and auction guides: buyers pay 30-70% less than new for used restaurant equipment, while sellers get only 10-30% of the original price. Half of this pack's $2,628 pair is taken. No warranty. 48 months of remaining life is my assumption (a 10-year unit bought at year 6). Older units may run on R-404A, a refrigerant that is being phased down, so a leak can cost more than the fridge.

setup.name: Refurbished espresso grinder
Certified installation of the espresso machine
setup.note: Three hours at $250, the on-site hourly rate on the price page of a New York City espresso service company (one-hour minimum, then billed by the quarter hour; established service departments elsewhere publish $130-$135 regular and $260 emergency). Covers the water line, drain, power hookup and calibration. Dealers void the warranty on a machine that was not installed by a certified technician with water treatment in place. Check the voltage first: a 240V heating element gives only about 75% of its power on a 208V building supply.

setup.name: Commercial blender with sound enclosure
Hot water dispenser for tea and americanos
Undercounter freezer
Countertop convection oven for baking off pastry
Panini grill
Commercial microwave
Ventless high-speed oven for hot sandwiches
Two-tap cold brew and nitro dispenser
Wireless temperature sensors for the fridges
setup.note: Three sensors at $28.99 and one hub at $39.99 = $126.96 (MOCREO list prices seen in search results; the basic cloud plan is free). Professional kits cost far more: a single Kitchen Brains sensor is about $182. The sensors text you when a fridge warms up overnight; they go blind if the Wi-Fi or power is out. 60 months is the IRS recovery period.

setup.name: Second, battery-powered card terminal
setup.note: Square Terminal: $299 on Square's hardware page (or $27 a month over 12 months); the home page showed $399 on the same day, so check the price at checkout. A second device keeps cards working when the register dies and can take payments offline.

setup.name: Replacement water heater (30-50 gallon tank, installed)
setup.note: Not an opening purchase when the space has a working heater. Replacement in New York: $2,400-$3,500 for a 50-gallon tank (HomeBlue, 2022) and $2,200-$4,400 on a 2026 plumber price page that adds a $280 Buildings Department permit and a $130 inspection; $3,300 is the middle. Tank water heaters last 8-12 years (ASHRAE figure for gas tank heaters); 10 taken. Without hot water at the hand sink you cannot legally serve.

setup.name: Scale inspection for selling beans by weight
setup.agency: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP)

setup.name: One-section reach-in freezer for frozen pastry
State food processing license (Article 20-C)
setup.agency: NYS Department of Agriculture and Markets

setup.name: Job ads for the opening team
setup.note: Search-seen (secondary): a sponsored job on Indeed needs a budget reported as $5 to $25 a day. My estimate: $25 a day for 12 days = $300 to fill four barista jobs. Free routes exist (a sign in the window, Instagram, asking your roaster) but take longer. Every ad must state the pay range (NYC Administrative Code 8-107(32) for employers of 4 or more, counting the owner).

setup.name: Paid working interviews (trial shifts)
setup.note: Arithmetic: 8 candidates x 3 hours x $17.00 = $408. A trial shift is work: search-seen (primary, NY DOL Hospitality Wage Order FAQ and Part 146): anyone who reports for duty at your request is owed at least 3 hours (or the scheduled shift if shorter) under 12 NYCRR 146-1.5. Eight candidates for four jobs is my assumption. Opened: Part 146, section 146-1.5 (three hours) and the NY DOL minimum wage page ($17.00).

setup.name: Food Protection Certificates for two shift leads
setup.note: Arithmetic: 2 leads x ($24 exam + 15 paid hours x $24) = $768. The exam fee and the 15 lessons are in the existing pack (seen there at NYC Health); one paid hour per lesson is my assumption, and study time you require is paid time. One certificate covers one person on one shift: a shop open 84 hours a week needs at least three holders (owner plus two) so that sickness or a day off never leaves a shift uncovered. Opened: NYC Health: the online course is free and has 15 lessons, the exam costs $24, and at least one certified supervisor must be on site whenever the establishment operates.

setup.name: Staff handbook and required written policies
setup.note: My estimate: two hours of an employment lawyer at $300 to adapt free state and city templates (harassment prevention policy, sick leave policy, tip pool rules, lactation policy). The $300 rate is a planning figure, not a quote. New York requires every employer, whatever its size, to adopt a harassment prevention policy and hand it over at hire (Labor Law 201-g); the state publishes a free model policy.

setup.name: Aprons and shirts for the team
setup.note: My estimate: 5 people x (2 aprons at $18 + 2 shirts at $12) = $300; prices are planning figures. Search-seen (primary, Part 146 and the DOL FAQ): the employer pays for required uniforms, and owes weekly uniform maintenance pay unless the uniform is wash-and-wear and enough pieces are supplied; two sets per person is the usual way to meet that exception.

setup.name: Workplace posters, 'Your Rights at Work' notice, harassment policy
setup.agency: NYS Department of Labor; NYC DCWP
setup.note: All required posters and the state's model harassment policy and training are free downloads from the agencies (NYS DOL posting requirements page; DCWP). The cost is $0 by design; mailers that bill $92.58 for a 'mandatory poster' are a known scam (BBB Scam Tracker). Should be required in every kit.

setup.name: Harassment prevention training for the opening team
setup.note: Arithmetic: 5 people x 1 paid hour x $21 = $105. The state's model training is free; the cost is the paid hour. Search-seen (secondary): Labor Law 201-g requires every employer to train every employee each year and to give the policy and training materials in writing at hire.

setup.name: Two rigid trash bins with secure lids
setup.note: Required since March 1, 2024 for every business that sets trash at the curb (opened NYC311: 'all businesses in NYC must use bins with secure lids'; 'The City does not sell or give away trash or recycling bins to commercial businesses'). Price is my planning value: two 44-gallon rigid bins with locking lids at about $90 each from a restaurant supplier. They live inside or within 3 feet of the building line and take about 8 square feet of floor.

setup.name: Snow shovel, ice scraper, salt spreader, four bags of ice melt
setup.note: Planning value: shovel $35, scraper $20, hand spreader $25, four 50 lb bags at about $20. Buy in November: stores ran out before the January and February 2026 storms. Not needed with the contractor option of snow_ice_plan.

setup.name: Two commercial entrance mats and wet-floor signs
setup.note: Alternative to the rented mats in the lever entrance_floor_safety: two 4 x 6 foot scraper mats at about $110 each and two signs at $20. Planning values.

setup.name: Dunnage racks: keep stock 6 inches off the basement floor
setup.note: Four racks at about $80 (planning value). Part of flood_protection = basic. The Health Code also requires food to be stored off the floor; the exact height and code number belong to D08.

setup.name: Required health signs and posters
setup.note: Seen at NYC Health: the choking first aid poster, CPR equipment notice, food allergy poster, no smoking sign and alcohol-pregnancy sign are free by calling 311. The $25 for frames and tape and the 5 days of mail are my estimate. Should be required in every kit: the lead or the assembler can flip the flag once kits include it.

setup.name: Allergy statement on menus and allergy poster for staff
setup.agency: NYS Department of Health / NYC DOHMH
setup.note: Public Health Law §1356: the notice must appear on each menu, on online ordering pages, and on a staff poster in the workers' languages. $60 to reprint a menu board and paper menus is my estimate; the poster is free. Should be required in every kit.

setup.name: No smoking and no vaping signs, written smoking policy
setup.note: NYC Health: owners must post the signs and adopt a written smoking and e-cigarette policy shared with staff. Signs are free from the city; $0 is by design.

setup.name: FDNY open flame permit (candles)
Sign permit and licensed sign hanger
setup.note: Seen at the Department of Buildings: a sign over 6 square feet needs a permit, and the installation must be done by a licensed sign hanger. The $1,500 for the filing, the hanger and the insurance certificate and the 30 days are my estimate; quotes vary widely. Not needed for a sign of 6 square feet or less. This is on top of the pack's $1,500 line for making the sign.

setup.name: Backflow device test and first report
setup.note: The yearly test report is the legal duty (15 RCNY §20-04(e), seen in the OATH penalty schedule). $240 per test is my estimate from plumbers' advertised ranges of $150 to $350. If the space has no device at all, installing one is plumbing work with filed plans and costs thousands: check before signing the lease.

setup.name: Portable ramp, doorbell and a lowered counter section
setup.note: My estimate: an aluminum portable ramp for one step ($300-$700), a wireless doorbell with a sign ($50), and carpentry for a 36-inch-high section of counter ($800). A small business gets back 50% of access spending between $250 and $10,250 as the federal Disabled Access Credit, up to $5,000 a year (IRS Form 8826): about $675 of this.

setup.name: Website and online menu a screen reader can use
setup.note: My estimate for a small site: text alternatives for images, a real text menu instead of a photo or PDF, labeled buttons, and a check with a screen reader. Why it matters: 3,117 federal website accessibility suits in 2025, 1,021 of them in New York (Seyfarth Shaw).

setup.name: Trademark search and federal application for the shop's name
setup.note: The search is free. The $350 filing fee per class and the roughly one year to registration are from memory of the 2025 USPTO fee schedule; I did not open it this session. Why it matters: a renamed Michigan cafe paid about $5,000 after a chain sued, against an estimated $50,000 to fight.

setup.name: Sales tax Certificate of Authority
setup.agency: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance
setup.note: Free; apply at least 20 days before the first taxable sale (existing _common roadmap step sales_tax_certificate). Added here as a setup item so that opening without it leaves a trail. Marked not required only so that the kits stay valid: the lead should add it to the kits and set required to true. The penalty for selling without it is taken from the existing pack; the penalty page opened this session showed only the $50 penalty for not displaying it.

setup.name: Free lease review (NYC Small Business Services)
setup.agency: NYC Department of Small Business Services
setup.note: The city offers free commercial lease help to small businesses; this item is the in-game hook that reveals the lease's renewal, termination and tax-escalation clauses before signing.

setup.name: Landlord's consent to assign the lease (landlord's legal fee)
setup.note: Only for buying an operating business. Key money deals assign the existing lease to the buyer, usually with the landlord's consent; landlords may ask for a rent bump, a higher deposit or a new guaranty (Commercial Observer, quoted in a search excerpt). No public figure for the fee or the time: $2,500 and 30 days are my estimates.

setup.name: Notice of a bulk sale to New York State (Form AU-196.10)
setup.agency: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance
setup.note: Only for buying an operating business. Quoted in search excerpts of NYS Tax Appeals determinations and the DTF bulletin: under Tax Law 1141(c) the buyer files AU-196.10 at least 10 days before paying for or taking possession of the business assets; the state answers within 5 business days (AU-196.2) and may claim the seller's unpaid sales tax within 90 days. A buyer who skips it becomes personally liable for the seller's unpaid sales tax.

kits.name: Lean start
kits.pitch: The legal minimum in a small room: 12 seats, one grinder, hand-washed cups, no sign. Cheapest way to open, but the room fills up at 170 orders a day.

kits.name: Standard
kits.pitch: The usual neighborhood cafe: 18 seats, drip coffee and iced drinks, a proper sign. Sized for 200 orders a day with room to spare.

kits.name: Premium
kits.pitch: 24 seats, a three-group machine, top grinders, a dishwasher and a customer restroom (required from 20 seats). Higher quality, about $29,000 more up front, and more seats to fill.

monthlyCosts.name: Rent
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: $90 per sq ft a year x 800 sq ft / 12 = $6,000, a moderate Brooklyn side street (REBNY 2025: small Park Slope spaces ask under $100). The game takes rent from the place on the map; this line is the fallback. See extra.rentByTier. D11 check (search-seen): REBNY Brooklyn retail report, first half of 2025, average asking rent on Smith Street $90 per sq ft (down 5%), Court Street $115; CoStar via Matthews puts the Brooklyn average at $54.60 in the second quarter of 2026. $90 is a corridor rent; a true side street is usually lower.

monthlyCosts.name: Electricity, gas, water and sewer
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: planning band $800-$1,800. Electricity alone at 3,000-5,000 kWh x 23.1 cents (NYSERDA statewide commercial average, August 2026) is $693-$1,155. The kWh figure is the notes' assumption.

monthlyCosts.name: Business owner's policy: liability, property, interruption
monthlyCosts.note: CORRECTION of the note, amount unchanged. Seen at Insureon (page updated autumn 2026): coffee shops pay on average $126 a month ($1,507 a year) for a business owner's policy, $82 a month for general liability alone, $88 a month for workers' compensation. These are US averages of one broker's small customers; the New York City reserve of $250 stays. Two things the old note missed: the liability part is priced on sales and trued up by a premium audit after the policy year (extra.mechanics.insurance_claims_and_audit), and business insurance for New York-area service firms rose 7% in the last year (Manhattan Chamber of Commerce, reported by Bloomberg and Insurance Journal, October 2026).

monthlyCosts.name: Cups, lids, sleeves, napkins, bags
monthlyCosts.note: Kept at $0.17; now built bottom-up. Opened at WebstaurantStore on November 14, 2026: hot set 11.7 cents (12 oz cup $45.99 per 1,000, lid $34.99 per 1,000, sleeve $43.49 per 1,200), cold set 9.8 cents (16 oz PET cup $59.49, strawless lid $38.49 per 1,000). With 111 drinks and 35 food items per 100 orders the packaging that leaves with the customer is 13.7 cents an order; napkins, wooden stirrers, sugar and straws on request add about 3.5 cents (my estimate). If the engine starts costing the menu item by item (extra.menu), cups are already inside each item's cogs: drop this line then, or it is counted twice.

monthlyCosts.name: Card processing: percentage fee
monthlyCosts.note: Seen in Square's fee table: 2.5% + 15 cents per tap on the Plus plan (2.6% on Free). Research notes model: 90% of sales on cards, and the percentage is charged on sales tax and tips too: 0.9 x 2.5% x 1.08875 + 2.5% x $2,000 of card tips / $51,000 of sales = 2.55% of sales.

monthlyCosts.name: Card processing: 15 cents per tap
monthlyCosts.note: 15 cents per card transaction (seen in Square's fee table) x 90% of orders paid by card = 13.5 cents per order. With the percentage fee the total is about 4.1% of sales on an $8.50 ticket.

monthlyCosts.name: Employer payroll tax on reported tips
monthlyCosts.note: Tips are wages for payroll tax (IRS Publication 15). Research notes assume $2,000 of card tips a month on $51,000 of sales: 7.65% x $2,000 = $153 = 0.3% of sales.

monthlyCosts.name: Paid sick leave cover
monthlyCosts.note: Up to 40 paid hours a year per worker for employers with 5-99 workers (DCWP): 40 h x $18 / 12 = $60 a month per worker when it is all used. Since February 22, 2026 every employer also owes 32 more hours of unpaid leave a year, available at once (DCWP adopted rules effective July 23, 2026, seen on rules.cityofnewyork.us), and 20 hours of paid prenatal leave a year under New York State law.

monthlyCosts.name: Small repairs: bulbs, door hardware, gaskets, fittings
monthlyCosts.note: D03 correction: the old $300 line bundled everything. It is now itemized below: grease interceptor pump-out, repair calls, backflow test, extinguisher service, burrs, cleaning chemicals and smallwares, while filter cartridges and preventive service are levers. What is left here is a $45 allowance for bulbs, door closers, fridge gaskets and fittings (my allowance, no public figure). All maintenance lines together come to about $480 a month before the levers, against $300 before.

monthlyCosts.name: Private carter: trash, recycling, organics
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: band $150-$400; not a city rate. Seen at the Sanitation Department: businesses sign with one of three carters authorized for their commercial waste zone, and each carter has a maximum price that depends on volume. D11 check (search-seen): the Business Integrity Commission customer guide (November 2024) lists maximum carter rates of $26.87 per cubic yard and $17.64 per 100 lb of trash, with mandatory discounts for recyclables and organics; carters must pick up trash at least twice a week. About 2 cubic yards a week (8.7 a month) at the cap is $234 before recycling and organics, so $250 is in range. Commercial Waste Zones: Queens Central from January 3, 2025, the Bronx from December 1, 2025, Staten Island and Midtown South noticed in August 2026, Brooklyn East, Manhattan Northeast, Queens West and Manhattan West in a 2026 rule; the whole city by the end of 2027 (DSNY waste equity report 2025). In a zone the shop must use the zone carter.

monthlyCosts.name: Internet and phone
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: band $80-$150; Verizon business internet starts at $69 a month plus fees.

monthlyCosts.name: POS software subscription
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: Square Plus $49 per location a month (Free plan $0, Premium $149). The plan prices were not readable on the page when I opened it.

monthlyCosts.name: Bookkeeping and year-end accountant
monthlyCosts.note: The inherited budget for bookkeeping plus year-end accounting is not verified by a matching QuickBooks Live tier. Provider scope excludes tax return filing and other tasks; subscription, onboarding and separate professional services require distinct quotes.

monthlyCosts.name: Payroll service
monthlyCosts.note: The inherited amount includes a planning buffer above the selected-person-count tariff calculation. The published fixed and per-person components are separately verified; the buffer is not a provider charge.

monthlyCosts.name: Website, listings, menus and printing
monthlyCosts.note: Research notes: chosen budget inside a $100-$600 band, not an industry norm.

monthlyCosts.name: Permit renewals and filing fees
monthlyCosts.note: The inherited monthly reserve is not an actual monthly fee. Food-service renewal, entity tax classification and any scale/sign obligations need separate applicable schedules; the state LLC filing amount is not universal.

monthlyCosts.name: Yearly backflow preventer test
monthlyCosts.note: City rule (15 RCNY §20-04, DEP): each backflow prevention assembly is tested at least once a year by a state-certified tester employed by a licensed master plumber, at the customer's expense, and the report is filed with DEP. No New York City price was found: $450 a year is taken from the $389-$559 quoted for New Rochelle (an upstate utility charges $100 per device) = $38 a month. Applies when DEP requires a device on your water service; DEP mails a letter when the test is due.

monthlyCosts.name: Grease interceptor pump-out
monthlyCosts.note: $75 a month is the saving this pack already gives for skipping the pump-out (shortcut skip_grease_trap_cleaning); it is taken out of the old maintenance line so the two agree. A New York cost guide lists commercial grease trap cleaning at $300-$800 a visit: about one visit every 4-10 months at this rate. The rule: grease may not fill more than 25% of the interceptor.

monthlyCosts.name: Repair calls: plumbing, refrigeration, espresso, air conditioning
monthlyCosts.note: Three service calls a year x $754.10, the average restaurant service request in 2024 (86 Repairs) = $2,262 a year = $189 a month. The number of calls is my planning assumption: no public statistic of repair calls per small cafe was found. By equipment (86 Repairs, 2021): reach-in refrigerator $519.05, plumbing $666.28, air conditioning $1,019.90; a technician on site costs $135 before any work. These are repairs that happen even with good care; breakdowns from skipped maintenance come on top.

monthlyCosts.name: Yearly fire extinguisher service and FDNY tags
monthlyCosts.note: FDNY: every extinguisher carries the FDNY tag and is serviced at least once a year by a W-96 certificate holder from an approved company. Price from one New York vendor list: $15-$25 per unit for 1-10 extinguishers plus a $50-$150 trip fee: 3 units x $20 + $100 = $160 a year = $13 a month.

monthlyCosts.name: Grinder burrs
monthlyCosts.note: Mahlkonig: E65S burr set $149.99, rated for about 800 kg. With 70% of orders taking a 20 g dose (my assumption) an order uses 0.014 kg: $149.99 / 800 x 0.014 = $0.0026 per order, about $16 a month at 6,000 orders. Dull burrs grind slower and hotter and the coffee tastes flat.

monthlyCosts.name: Espresso machine, grinder and brewer cleaners
monthlyCosts.note: Backflush powder: Urnex Cafiza 20 oz $9.69 (WebstaurantStore), about one jar a month at 16 g a day; grinder cleaner: Urnex Grindz $25.99 (urnex.com), one jar per quarter = $8.70; descaler for the brewer: Dezcal 1 liter $15.99 per quarter = $5.30. Total about $24 a month. Usage is my estimate from the dosing on the labels.

monthlyCosts.name: Broken and lost smallwares
monthlyCosts.note: This pack's own figures: $2,000 of pitchers, cups, tampers, scales and bins with a 24-month life = $83 a month. It was part of the old maintenance line.

monthlyCosts.name: Replacing staff who leave
monthlyCosts.note: Arithmetic: 50% of the team leaves in a year x $2,706 to replace one hourly worker / 12 = $113 per worker a month. Search-seen (secondary): Black Box Intelligence 2025 puts the hard cost (separation, recruiting, training) at $2,706 per hourly restaurant worker, up from about $2,300 in 2024, and yearly turnover of limited-service hourly staff near 110%. Search-seen (primary, bls.gov JOLTS): the monthly quits rate in accommodation and food services ran 3.6% to 5.0% between June and September 2026, 43% to 60% a year. I take 50% for a small owner-run shop. A fuller count that includes lost output is $5,864 (Cornell Center for Hospitality Research, older study). The engine should replace this flat line with extra.mechanics.turnover_and_replacement.

monthlyCosts.name: Overtime premiums for covering absences
monthlyCosts.note: Arithmetic: 4.0% of 160 hours = 6.4 hours a worker misses each month; if half of them are covered by a colleague already at 40 hours, 3.2 h x $10.50 (the half-time premium on $21) = $34. Search-seen (secondary, quoting BLS): food preparation and serving workers had a 4.0% absence rate in 2025, against 3.2% for all workers. The 50% share is my assumption.

monthlyCosts.name: Shift drinks for staff
monthlyCosts.note: My estimate: 2 drinks a shift x 20 shifts x $0.90 of ingredients = $36 per worker a month. A free coffee is not a "meal" under the Hospitality Wage Order, so nothing can be taken off wages for it (12 NYCRR 146-1.9 allows a credit only for a full meal).

monthlyCosts.name: Scheduling and time clock app
monthlyCosts.note: Search-seen (secondary, vendor comparison checked October 2026): Homebase Basic is free for one location, Essentials is $30 a month, Plus $70. The app keeps the time records that New York requires you to hold for six years (12 NYCRR 146-2.1); with no records, the worker's own account of hours is believed.

monthlyCosts.name: Paid yearly trainings
monthlyCosts.note: Arithmetic: 3 paid hours a year x $21 / 12 = $5.25 per worker a month: one hour of harassment prevention training (required every year, Labor Law 201-g) and two hours of food safety and allergen refreshers (my assumption).

monthlyCosts.name: Business checking account and cash deposit fees
monthlyCosts.note: Secondary sources on Chase Business Complete Checking, 2026: $15 a month, waived with a $2,000 minimum daily balance; the first $5,000 of cash deposits per statement cycle is free, then about $2.50-$3 per $1,000 (sources differ; the bank's own fee schedule was not readable). A shop with 10% of $51,000 in cash deposits about $5,100 a month, right at the limit. Planning value: $15 fee in thin months plus a few dollars of deposit and change-order fees = $20.

monthlyCosts.name: Refunds and card disputes
monthlyCosts.note: Seen at Square: a disputed amount is held at once, the seller has 7 days to answer, the bank may take up to 90 days, there is no dispute fee, and the processing fee is not returned when the customer wins. No public statistic of dispute or refund rates for coffee shops was found; tap-and-go disputes are rare. Planning value: 0.1% of sales ($51 a month at $51,000), mostly refunded remakes and double charges.

staff.name: Barista
staff.note: NY Department of Labor OEWS file (wages updated to the first quarter of 2026), New York City region, SOC 35-3023 Fast Food and Counter Workers, the occupation that holds baristas: median $36,545.83 a year ($17.57 an hour at 2,080 hours), mean $39,310.12 ($18.90), entry $35,510.25 ($17.07). OEWS wages include tips. A shop that pays the full $17.00 minimum with no tip credit and lets baristas keep their tips pays $17-$19; $18 is my middle. The research notes planned $21, which is above the market median even before tips. The tipped rate of $11.35 + $5.65 credit is legal only with written notice and tips that cover the gap (12 NYCRR 146-1.3).

staff.note: D11: D05 set the pay ladder against a $21 barista (trainee $18, part-time $19). D12 moved the barista to $18 (NY DOL OEWS Q1 2026, NYC, SOC 35-3023: median $17.57, entry $17.07). The ladder is kept in order: a new barista starts at the NYC minimum wage, $17.00 (NY DOL; no increase on January 1, 2027).

staff.name: Part-time barista (20 hours a week)
staff.note: D11: D05 had $19 against a $21 barista; with the D12 barista wage of $18 a part-timer is paid the same hourly rate (part-time work in New York carries no separate minimum).

staff.name: Counter and register
staff.note: Search-seen (primary, bls.gov): cashiers in the New York metro averaged $17.67 an hour in May 2023; search-seen (secondary, BLS May 2025 data republished by WageDex): New York State cashiers, median $35,500 a year = $17.07 an hour. $17.50 is my rounding, 50 cents above the 2026 city minimum of $17.00. Takes orders and payment, plates pastries; does not pull shots, so peak drink output does not rise (extra.staffModel.stations). Serves customers, so shares in the tip pool.

staff.name: Dishwasher and porter
staff.note: Search-seen (secondary, BLS May 2025 data republished by WageDex): dishwashers in the New York metro, median $35,670 a year = $17.15 an hour; search-seen (primary, bls.gov): $16.75 median in May 2023. $17.25 is my rounding. Back-of-house: no customer service, so not eligible for the tip pool under the Hospitality Wage Order (12 NYCRR 146-2.14). 100 hours covers the midday rush and closing six days a week (my assumption).

staff.name: Baker and food prep
staff.note: Search-seen (primary, bls.gov): bakers in the New York metro, median $18.00 an hour in May 2023. The city minimum wage rose from $15.00 in 2023 to $17.00 in 2026 (+13%); $18.00 x 1.11 = $20, my estimate for 2026. Needed only if you bake or make sandwiches in-house; starts at 4 or 5 am. Not customer-facing, so outside the tip pool.

staff.name: Assistant manager (hourly)
staff.licenseRequired: NYC Food Protection Certificate (free online course, $24 exam)
staff.note: My estimate: between the shift lead ($24) and the lowest overtime-exempt salary in New York City in 2026, $1,275 a week, which is $31.88 an hour over 40 hours (search-seen, secondary, several law firms agree). Paid hourly because the salary is under that threshold: every hour over 40 in a week costs $40.50. 173 hours = 40 hours x 4.33 weeks. Hires, schedules and disciplines, so may not take any share of the tips (Labor Law 196-d; 29 U.S.C. 203(m)(2)(B)).

taxes.name: Income tax on the gain when you sell the business
taxes.appliesIf: only in the year you sell the business or its assets
taxes.note: IRS closing-a-business checklist: the sale is reported on Form 8594 (price split by asset class) and Form 4797. Equipment that was written off (section 179 or 100% bonus depreciation, IRS Publication 946) comes back as ordinary income when sold; goodwill held over a year is a long-term capital gain (federal 0% or 15% for this owner). New York State and City tax every gain as ordinary income, and UBT applies to the gain too. My blended planning rate for the exit mechanic: 28% of the gain (federal 12-22% ordinary on recaptured equipment or 15% on goodwill, state 5.4%, city 3.876%, UBT up to 4%). Not a quote; an accountant computes it from the allocation.

options.label: Staff clean every day, deep clean once a month
options.note: My estimate: staff clean during paid shifts; $130 is chemicals, paper and one monthly deep clean. No NYC tariff exists.

options.label: Professional cleaning crew every night
options.note: My estimate: a crew a few nights a week on top of staff cleaning, $400 more than standard. Seen through search: vendor prices for small NYC commercial spaces start at $150-$500 a month for an office up to 1,000 sq ft, and restaurant cleaning runs $50-$150 an hour for a professional crew; nightly restaurant service would cost more than this option. Not a quote.

options.label: Wipe and go
options.note: My estimate: $30 of supplies. Leads to dirty_surfaces: $200-$300 and 5-8 points per citation (Appendix 23-C, code 06D).

options.label: House blend from a wholesale roaster
Specialty roaster and local dairy
options.note: My arithmetic: about 108 kg (238 lb) of beans a month for 6,000 orders at 18 g, times about $3 more per lb for a specialty roaster = $714, rounded to $750 with local dairy. The $3 premium is my estimate; retail ground coffee averaged $9.25 per lb in October 2026 (BLS via FRED).

levers.name: Opening hours

options.label: 7am - 7pm
7am - 3pm: close after lunch
6am - 9pm
options.note: D11: was $2300. D12 recalculated the long-hours option with the D12 barista wage: 90 more paid hours x $18 x 1.116 employer taxes = $1,808 plus about $200 of power and supplies = about $2,000 (was $2,300 at $21). D06 options kept (it added the short day).

levers.note: Existing lever, same id; adds the option real owners use most: closing after lunch. On the neighborhood hour curve (extra.hourCurve) the hours from 3pm to 7pm carry 23% of the day's orders (16% in an office district). The option costs nothing by itself: its saving is that the shop can run with one barista fewer, about $3,860 a month in wages and payroll taxes for 160 hours at $21. At 200 orders a day the lost afternoon is worth more than that barista (1,380 orders x $8.50 x 68% = about $7,960 of contribution); under about 100 orders a day closing early wins. Owners' accounts: a Santa Barbara cafe dropped its evening hours once payroll and cleaning were counted against the sales; an upstate New York chain cut weekdays to a 2pm close. The long option is unchanged.

options.label: Licensed exterminator, monthly visits
options.note: Seen through search (vendor pages, not quotes): monthly contracts for small NYC restaurants run about $150-$300. $175 sits in that band. The Health Code requires a contract with a state-licensed exterminator and its records on site (§81.23(b)).

options.label: Skip it
Market wage
$2 an hour above market
options.note: My arithmetic: $2 x 160 h x 4 baristas = $1,280 x 1.116 employer taxes = $1,428, rounded to $1,430. The quality and capacity effects are game estimates.

levers.name: Laptops and Wi-Fi

options.label: Laptops welcome, free Wi-Fi all day
No laptops at lunch and on weekends
No Wi-Fi, outlets covered, screens off the tables
No laptops on weekends
One order per 90 minutes

levers.note: seatTurnsMult multiplies sizing.unitsServedPerSizeMonth (new field, see extra.mechanics seat_camping_dwell_mix). Derivation: with 30% of seated guests staying 120 minutes and 70% staying 35, the mean stay is 60 minutes; removing the long stays at peak hours brings it to about 50 (x1.2 turns), removing them all day to about 43 (x1.4). Demand losses are my estimates: seated laptop guests are about 12% of all orders (40% seated x 30%), and a part of them goes elsewhere. A real owner's account (NPR, 2014): a bakery cafe that switched off Wi-Fi and then banned screens at lunch saw sales rise, because people had been walking in, finding no table and leaving.

levers.name: Seating layout

options.label: Two-tops about two feet apart (18 sq ft per seat)
Squeeze the tables together (15 sq ft per seat)
One communal table and a window bar
Sofas and armchairs (22 sq ft per seat)
Two-tops instead of four-tops
Window bar rail for solo guests
Keep a 36-inch route to counter and toilet

levers.note: seatsFitMult multiplies how many seats the address holds (18 / 15 = 1.2; 18 / 22 = 0.82). Evidence for the quality loss: Cornell field study in a New York restaurant (Robson and Kimes, 2009): guests at tables 20 inches or less apart were less satisfied in almost every category and less likely to return, although they left sooner; a 2011 survey of more than 1,000 Americans found strong objection to tables 6 and 12 inches apart. Communal seating raises turns because a solo guest takes one chair instead of a table for two or four. Lounge numbers are my estimates.

levers.name: Line and pickup

options.label: One register, the line forms where it can
Marked line, menu readable from the door, separate pickup shelf
Order-ahead by phone with a pickup shelf

levers.note: Evidence: a supermarket deli study (Lu, Musalem, Olivares, Schilkrut, Management Science 2013) found that shoppers react to how long the line looks, not to how fast it moves, and that the effect on buying is strong and non-linear; the working paper put a moderately longer line on a par with a 5% price rise. So a line that looks short (hidden bend, people waiting at pickup instead of in the queue) loses fewer buyers. Order-ahead costs bar capacity: Starbucks said a mid-teens percent of its mobile orders went uncompleted in spring 2024 because bars could not keep up. The effect sizes and monthly costs are game values.

levers.name: Restroom access

options.label: Customers only: door code printed on the receipt
Open to anyone who asks
No public restroom (legal only under 20 seats)

levers.note: The law, read in both codes: under 20 seats a food business owes customers no restroom (Health Code 81.22(b); Plumbing Code 403.3, exception 1), and NYC311 adds that food businesses need not open their employee toilets to the public; at 20 or more it must provide one, free of charge. The engine should refuse staff_only at 20 or more seats or attach the violation no_patron_toilet. Starbucks ended its open-door restroom policy on January 27, 2025 and now requires a purchase (press, search excerpt). The $150 for extra paper, soap and cleaning is my estimate.

Wait until it breaks

levers.name: Cold-proofing the shop

options.label: Turn the heat down at night and hope
Insulated pipes, heat held at 55°F overnight, door closer and draft strip
All of that plus a temporary winter vestibule at the door, November 15 to April 15

levers.note: pipes_and_door: $150 of pipe insulation and weather-stripping and a $120 door closer over five cold months, plus about $40 a month of extra heat = $70 (planning values). vestibule: a sign maker's guide says a temporary storm enclosure may stand from November 15 to April 15, may project 18 inches for most businesses and up to 25 square feet for restaurants if 5 feet of sidewalk stay clear (Building Code §3202.3.2.1), and needs no Buildings Department permit inside those limits; the official text was not opened. $450 a month = a made-to-measure vinyl and aluminum vestibule with installation, removal and storage at about $2,250 a season (my planning value; get quotes), plus the $70. It keeps the tables by the door usable (door_draft_tables) and gives the queue a place out of the wind. 'none' decides whether frozen_pipe hits the shop: water and freezing damage is 20% of small-business claims and averages $34,600 (The Hartford, 2025).

levers.name: Seats outside

options.label: No outdoor seats
Licensed sidewalk cafe: 4 tables against your wall
Licensed roadway cafe in the parking lane, now allowed all year

levers.note: Sidewalk: license $1,050 for four years ($22 a month) plus the yearly consent fee, $6 a square foot in about 80% of the city (up to $31 in Manhattan below 125th Street): 100 sq ft x $6 / 12 = $50; furniture $1,100 written off over four years = $23. Total $95 at the $6 rate; at $31 the fee alone is $258 a month. Roadway: license $22 a month; consent fee $5-$25 a square foot (160 sq ft x $8 / 12 = $107); a code-compliant platform and barriers of about $7,000 over two years = $290. The roadway numbers other than the fee range are my planning values. Seats count only on dry days between about 55°F and 88°F (extra.mechanics.outdoor_seat_days). The existing rule card says approval took most applicants over 19 months, and outdoor seats count toward the 20-seat bathroom line. Since August 31, 2026 roadway cafes may stay up all year under a separate license; the winter rules are still being written.

levers.name: Music

options.label: Slow, quiet playlist
Faster playlist at peak hours

levers.note: Evidence: Milliman (Journal of Consumer Research, 1986) found restaurant guests stay longer under slow music with no change in food spending; a 2024 field experiment in a restaurant measured 80 minutes under slow music against 57 under fast, with no significant difference in the bill. The 10% either way for a cafe is my estimate. Licensing the music is a separate cost (see D08).

Leave the step as it is

levers.note: Only for an address with a step at the door. The ramp is the setup item portable_entrance_ramp ($157). Federal law asks an existing business to remove barriers where that is readily achievable. IRS Form 8826, read: a business with gross receipts of $1 million or less or no more than 30 full-time employees gets a credit of 50% of its access spending between $250 and $10,250 a year, at most $5,000.

levers.note: $431 = $45 + $257 employment practices + $129 cyber (both seen at Insureon). The $45 for the three endorsements is a planning value with no public price behind it: insurers quote them case by case. What each option covers is in the covers list of event ids; nothing here covers a flood (separate federal flood policy) or unpaid wages.

levers.name: Pastry

options.label: Baked pastries delivered before opening
Bake frozen pastry in the shop through the morning
Hire a baker and bake from scratch
Drinks only, no food

levers.note: At the reference month (6,000 orders): 780 croissants, 420 muffins, 300 cookies and 360 bagels sold, $3,564 of bakery bought, $394 of it thrown away. Bake-off: a delivered croissant costs $2.43 per one sold after 12% waste, a frozen ready-to-bake one $1.50 after 6% waste (price seen at WebstaurantStore), so croissants alone save $725 a month; muffin batter and cookie dough are assumed to save another $600 (not checked). Against that: 45 minutes of staff time a day ($420 a month with payroll taxes) and about $80 of electricity and parchment. Net about -$900. Scratch baking: ingredients fall to about a quarter of the shelf price (saves about $1,400 on $8,400 of bakery sales) but a baker at $22 an hour for 120 hours costs $2,900 with payroll taxes: net +$1,500, and it needs a kitchen the notes' format does not have. A negative monthlyCost is a saving. 'Drinks only' removes about 16% of sales (bakery is $1.40 of a $7.75 order); the engine has no field for ticket size, so it is written as -5% demand.

levers.name: Oat and almond milk

options.label: $1 extra for plant milk
Plant milk at no extra charge
Dairy only

levers.note: Oat milk costs 10.4 cents an ounce against 4.1 for dairy (both seen): 63 cents more per 12 oz latte. With the upcharge, 10 of 100 orders are oat drinks. Without it I assume oat rises to a third of milk drinks (Square, 2024: oat is in 33% of orders with milk), 22 of 100 orders: 600 lost upcharges ($600) plus 720 more oat drinks at 63 cents ($454) = $1,050 a month at 6,000 orders. Starbucks dropped its 70-80 cent charge on November 7, 2024 and said nearly half of its US customers order plant milk, so a customer now meets the charge mostly at independents. Dairy only: no cartons to waste (-$150) but every tenth order walks.

levers.name: Unsold food at closing

options.label: Throw it away
Sell it in surprise bags through a surplus-food app
Donate it to a food rescue group
Staff take it home

levers.note: About 223 unsold items a month with a shelf value of $900. Too Good To Go: the shop packs surplus into a bag priced at a third of its value ($300 a month) and pays an annual fee plus a fee per bag; the only US figure found is 'about 25%' (2023 press), so $225 is kept. Payouts come quarterly. Donation: the federal Good Samaritan Food Donation Act shields a good-faith donor from liability unless grossly negligent, and Internal Revenue Code §170(e)(3) gives an enhanced deduction; the money value of the deduction is left out. The fourth real option, selling it tomorrow, is the existing shortcut keep_old_food.

levers.name: How much fresh food to order

options.label: Enough for a normal day: about one in eight left over
Order to sell out by mid-afternoon
A full case until closing

levers.note: Standard: 12% of bakery unsold (trade guide: 10-15%), $394 a month at cost. Tight: 4% unsold saves $270, but an empty case after 2 pm loses about 8% of $8,415 bakery sales: $673 of sales, $337 of margin. The saving and the loss are nearly equal, which is the lesson: wasted pastry is cheap, a missed sale is not. Abundant: 22% unsold, $894 thrown away, $500 more than standard. Demand effects are design values.

levers.name: Coffee price

options.label: Pay the roaster's current price list
Lock today's price for 12 months against a volume commitment

levers.note: The reference shop buys about 269 lb of coffee a month ($4,100), a third of its cost of goods. A lock is free to sign and cuts both ways: someone who locked in late 2025, with the exchange near $3.90 a lb, was still paying that level in November 2026 with the exchange at $2.80. Roasters themselves buy forward; whether a given roaster will hold a price for a small cafe is a matter of negotiation, not a published tariff. Engine: while the lock runs, coffee events in either direction do not touch this shop.

levers.name: How supplies reach the shop

options.label: One cafe distributor delivers overnight
Owner drives to the cash-and-carry warehouse every week
Keep a second supplier on every key item

levers.note: Dry goods, plant milk and disposables are about $2,200 a month at the reference volume. Cash-and-carry: I assume 8% cheaper ($177) against four trips at about $34 each for the $9 congestion toll, fuel and parking ($136): the trip saves almost nothing in cash and costs the owner 12 hours a month off the floor. Second supplier: split orders lose volume discounts and meet two minimums; $120 is my estimate. In exchange, events tagged supplier_failure do not empty the shelves.

levers.name: Counting stock

options.label: Count once a month
Weekly count against the register, recipes in the POS
Order by eye, never count

levers.note: Shrink (free drinks for friends, unrecorded staff drinks, remakes, over-pouring, product that walks out the back) is taken as 2% of sales with a monthly count, 1% with a weekly count and 4% with none. On $51,000 of sales: weekly saves $510 and costs $260 of a shift lead's time, net -$250; no counting costs $1,020 more. The 4% is the figure the trade repeats and attributes to the National Restaurant Association (theft about 4% of sales, employees behind about 75% of inventory shortages); I found it only in vendor blogs, so all three levels are estimates.

levers.name: Cups

options.label: Plain stock cups
Custom-printed cups with your logo
Compostable cups and lids

levers.note: About 6,660 cups a month. Compostable: the hot cup alone is 7.8 cents against 4.6 (both pages opened), and with a compostable lid I take 4.5 cents more per set: $300. Custom print: about 4 cents more per cup at small runs (my estimate): $265. Printers' terms seen: one case of 500-1,000 with 3-4 weeks' lead time at one supplier; 50 cases and 14-19 weeks at another; 30,000 paper cups and 12 weeks at a third. A sticker or stamp on a stock cup is the cheap version. Compostable cups in New York end up in the trash unless the carter collects organics.

levers.name: What goes in the takeout bag

options.label: Straws, forks and napkins only when the customer asks
Everything in every bag, no questions

levers.note: $25 a month of extra straws, forks and napkins is my estimate. The legal option is also the cheaper one; the illegal one only saves a few seconds per order.

levers.name: Seasonal drinks

options.label: Same menu all year
A seasonal special every quarter

levers.note: $250 a month for sauces, toppings, a menu reprint and the unsold seasonal stock written off when the season ends (my estimate). The 3% is a design value; the only measured figure is for a chain with national advertising: Starbucks visits on its fall launch day, August 25, 2026, were 25.7% above its daily average for the year (Placer.ai). A seasonal latte sells for $1.25 more than a plain one with 34 cents of extra ingredients.

levers.name: Milk for drip coffee

options.label: Staff add milk behind the counter
Self-serve carafes, time-labelled and swapped every 4 hours
Carafes sit on the bar from open to close

levers.note: NYC Health: cold food may be held without temperature control for 4 hours if labelled with the time it came out and the time to discard it, and must then be thrown away. Three swaps a day waste about a pint of milk and half-and-half each: 36 cents a pint x 3 x 30 = $32, plus labels: $45 (my arithmetic). Carafes left out all day are the existing violation spoiled_food ($250-$600).

levers.name: Shelf-stable stock on hand

options.label: One week of cups, plant milk, syrups and matcha
Six weeks on the shelf

levers.note: Dry goods, plant milk and disposables run about $2,200 a month at the reference volume, so five extra weeks is about $2,800 of cash sitting in boxes: 24 cases of oat milk, 8 cases of cups, lids and sleeves. $60 a month covers shelving and the odd case that goes out of date (my estimate). The catch is space: in 800 sq ft the boxes take the place of two seats or a staff corner. Events tagged shortage do not empty the shelves of a shop that holds six weeks.

levers.name: Deliveries before opening

options.label: Drivers have a key and a code and stock the fridge
Someone comes in an hour early to receive and check
Crates are left at the door

levers.note: Milk and pastry arrive between 3 am and 7 am. An extra paid hour a day at $17 plus payroll taxes is $580 a month. A key drop costs nothing but nobody checks temperatures, counts or dates at the door (the small quality loss is a design value). Crates on the sidewalk warm above 41°F on any mild morning and are sometimes gone by opening: that is the existing violation spoiled_food.

levers.name: Trash pickup

options.label: Ask all three zone carters and sign the cheapest
Miss the deadline and take the assigned carter at the maximum rate
Three pickups a week instead of six

levers.note: The pack budgets $250 a month. At the caps a shop putting out 40 lb a day pays about $322 in a $110-a-month zone (see suppliers.waste_carter), so 'assigned at the maximum' is about $70 above a negotiated contract. Fewer pickups save part of the frequency charge (my estimate $60) and leave food waste in the shop for two days: smell and pest pressure, written as a small quality loss.

levers.name: Cold brew

options.label: A measured batch every evening for tomorrow
Big batches twice a week, always in stock

levers.note: Cold brew steeps 12 to 24 hours, so tomorrow's supply is decided today. A measured daily batch runs out on the first hot afternoon; big batches never run out but about one batch in ten is poured away when it passes its week (12 servings x 81 cents x 4.5 = $45 a month, my arithmetic). In the iced season the event iced_season penalises the daily batch.

levers.name: Sandwiches, parfaits and bottled cold brew

options.label: Everything is made and wrapped after the customer orders
Packed in the morning for the fridge, each with an allergen label
Packed in the morning, no labels

levers.note: NY Agriculture and Markets Law §199-g, opened on the State Senate site on November 14, 2026 ('Effective November 12, 2026'): food prepared, prepacked and sold on the same premises must carry a label naming any major food allergen; food packaged after the customer has ordered is not covered. $35 a month is label stock and ten minutes each morning (my estimate). Packing ahead with no label is the third option and the violation allergen_label_missing.
