levers.name: Order-ahead

options.label: Counter orders only
Order-ahead on your own page, pickup slots capped in the rush
Order-ahead with no cap

levers.note: Cost: Square Online's free plan charges 3.3% + 30 cents on an online order against the pack's 2.55% + 13.5 cents at the counter: about 23 cents more on a $9.25 ticket with tax. With 10% of 6,000 orders placed ahead: 600 x $0.234 = $140; with no cap 800 orders = $190. Demand lifts are my estimates (a third of the order-ahead tickets counted as new). The capacity loss of the uncapped option is the Starbucks lesson of 2017: when a fifth of rush orders came by phone, the crowd at the handoff made walk-in customers turn around. Shares elsewhere: Starbucks 33% of transactions, Dutch Bros 11.5-14%.

levers.name: Delivery apps

options.label: No delivery
One app, basic listing: 15% delivery fee plus processing
Two apps with paid placement: 25-30% and more

levers.note: A fixed monthly cost stands in for a commission the format cannot express (extra.mechanics channel_margins has the real math). Basic: delivery sales of 5% of $51,000 = $2,550 a month; the app keeps 15% + 3% processing = $459, plus about $70 of bags and carriers = $530. Promoted: 9% = $4,590; 28% = $1,285, plus $135 of packaging = $1,420. New York City caps, read on the city's page: delivery fees 15% of each online order, transaction fees 3%, basic service fees 5%, enhanced service fees 20%, and 'the enhanced service fee can only be charged if the app offers a plan at a basic service fee amount'; apps cannot charge for phone orders that do not end in a sale. DoorDash's own page: 15% on delivery for Basic, 25% for Plus, 30% for Premier, 6% on pickup, no monthly fee and no contract, and a commission refund for a month with fewer than 20 accepted orders. Sales shares are estimates under the 9% that delivery holds in limited-service traffic nationally.

levers.name: Loyalty program

options.label: None
Paper punch card: the tenth drink is free
Digital loyalty on the register, points by phone number

levers.note: Punch card: 15% of 6,000 orders stamped = 900; a tenth are free: 90 drinks x $2.21 of ingredients = $199, plus $20 of printing. Digital: Square Loyalty costs $45 a month per location up to 500 loyalty visits, $75 up to 1,500, $105 above; with 30% of orders enrolled (1,800 visits) the fee is $105 and 180 free drinks cost $398: about $500. Demand lifts are deliberately small: Square reports enrolled coffee customers spending 1.67 times as much and visiting 57% more often, but that is a seller describing customers who were already its best ones.

levers.name: Online reviews

options.label: Leave the listings alone
Answer every review within two days, keep hours and photos current
Answer every review and put a review QR card on the counter

levers.note: Hotels that began answering reviews gained 0.12 stars (Proserpio and Zervas, 2017); at one star = 0.25 of the reputation scale that is +0.03. Asking adds volume, my estimate +0.01: Google allows asking; Yelp's filter tends to drop reviews a business asked for; a reward for a good review is a federal violation (see shortcut reward_good_reviews). The money cost is zero and the real cost is the owner's hour a week, which the game does not price. $20 is the printed cards.

levers.name: Rush-hour schedule

options.label: The same crew all day
Stagger shifts so two people work the bar from 7 to 10
Split shifts around the morning and afternoon rush

levers.note: The engine counts capacity by the month; a cafe loses its sales by the hour. At 200 orders a day the 8am hour brings 28 orders (36 in an office district) against about 25 an hour from one barista on the bar, so a flat crew turns people away at 8am while standing idle at 3pm. Overlap moves hours, not money. Split shifts stretch a worker's day past ten hours from start to finish, and New York's hospitality wage order then adds one hour at the minimum wage for that day: $17 x 2 workers x 30 days = $1,020. Capacity gains are my estimates of the rush orders saved, as a share of the day.

levers.name: Ordering kiosk

options.label: Orders at the register only
One self-order kiosk by the door

levers.note: Square's kiosk, launched October 14, 2026: $1,999 for the device with a counter stand plus $99 a month of software per device, and it needs the Plus plan ($49 a month, already in the pack as pos_software). $1,999 over 36 months = $56, plus $99 = $155 a month. The gain is at the rush: the person who took orders can move to the bar. 5% of the day's capacity is my estimate; no measurement of kiosk ticket size or share of orders was found (Square does not publish one). App-first chains in New York already order this way.

levers.name: Menu size

options.label: Espresso drinks, drip, tea, a pastry case
Short menu: no blended drinks, nothing made to order
Everything: blended drinks, matcha, toasts

levers.note: Speed against reach. A straight espresso takes about a minute and a milk drink two; blended and made-to-order items take longer and block the bar. Starbucks said in January 2025 it would cut about 30% of its food and drink items by the end of the fiscal year to shorten waits. The wide menu's $350 is extra spoilage and prep supplies, my estimate. All effect sizes are estimates.

levers.name: Office catering

options.label: None
Coffee boxes for offices: your own orders plus a catering marketplace

levers.note: 45 boxes a month at $30 = $1,350 = 2.6% of the reference sales, rounded to 0.03. Two thirds come through ezCater: 15% of food and delivery fee + 2.99% payment fee = 18% of $900 = $162; boxes, cups and lids for 45 kits at $3.50 = $158. A 96 oz box holds about ten 10 oz cups; Dunkin's sells for $22-$35 depending on the store. From 2026 ezCater also charges $2.25 for each order delivered without tracking. Volumes are my estimate for a shop near offices.

levers.name: Card fees at the counter

options.label: One price; you pay the card fees
Post a cash price and a card price side by side

levers.note: The negative cost is recovered fees: $51,000 x 90% paid by card x 60% of that on credit cards x 2.6% = $716. New York General Business Law section 518 (in force since February 11, 2024): the posted price must already be the total card price, the difference may not exceed what the processor charges you, and it applies to credit cards only, not debit. New York City also forbids charging more for cash and forbids a restaurant from adding a surcharge line to listed prices (6 RCNY section 5-59), so two posted prices is the only lawful form. Customers dislike it: J.D. Power found 81% of card users have switched payment method to dodge a surcharge and warns of 'acute abandonment risk'; the 3% demand loss is my estimate.

levers.name: Entry price

options.label: Drip coffee priced like everything else
Keep a $3 drip coffee on the board

levers.note: The answer to a cart at the subway stairs or a chain's $1.99 app coupon. Cost: 30% of 6,000 orders are drip (my estimate); cutting it from $3.75 to $3.00 gives up $0.75 x 1,800 = $1,350 a month. Toast's median price of a drip coffee was $3.65 in February 2026. The 5% lift is my estimate; at the reference shop it adds about $1,730 of contribution, so the move pays only when someone is actually undercutting you.

levers.name: Evenings

options.label: Nothing after closing
One event a week: run club, open mic or a tasting

levers.note: A planning value with no measurement behind it: $250 covers a paid hour of two staff and supplies four times a month. Owners describe events as the cheapest way to be known on the block; no study of the effect on sales was found.

levers.name: Snow and ice at your door

options.label: Staff shovel and salt on the clock, within the legal window
options.note: D11: was $90. D07 prices are per winter month (December-March). The engine charges levers every month, so the cost is spread over 12 months: 90 x 4 / 12 = 30, 400 x 4 / 12 = 133. Back to 90 and 400 once levers can have active months (D07 activeMonths).

options.label: Seasonal contract: a crew clears and salts after every snowfall
options.note: D11: was $400. D07 prices are per winter month (December-March). The engine charges levers every month, so the cost is spread over 12 months: 90 x 4 / 12 = 30, 400 x 4 / 12 = 133. Back to 90 and 400 once levers can have active months (D07 activeMonths).

options.label: Leave it: the sun will melt it

levers.note: Charged only in December-March (activeMonths is a new field). Staff option: Central Park averages about 11 days a season with measurable snow (1991-2020 normals in ai/src/data/nyc-climate.json: Dec 2.1, Jan 3.7, Feb 3.2, Mar 2.0), about 2.75 a month; one hour of a $17.00 worker each time plus a second pass for refreeze = 2.75 x 1.5 h x $17 = $70, plus about $20 of ice melt. Contractor: no New York storefront price was found; vendor guides quote $350-$1,500 per visit for commercial lots in Brooklyn and $2,000-$10,000 a season nationally, which is plowing, not a 20-foot sidewalk. $400 a month ($1,600 a season) is my planning value for a shovel-only sidewalk contract: get three local quotes. The summons is $100 per snowfall and $350 if ignored (OATH data). The -3% demand of 'none' applies only on days with snow or ice on the ground (see extra.mechanics.sidewalk_clock).

levers.name: Wet floor at the entrance

options.label: Rented entrance mats swapped weekly, wet-floor signs, mop every hour in bad weather
options.note: D11: was $80. D07 had $80 without a price list; D14 found about $5 a mat a week (2 mats x 5 x 52 / 12 = $43, chainstoreage.com vendor estimate).

options.label: A towel by the door

levers.note: No price list for mat rental in New York was found; $80 a month (two mats, weekly swap) is my planning value from uniform-service quotes I could not open. The reason the lever exists is the insurer's number: The Hartford's 2025 ten-year review puts the average slip, fall or customer injury claim of a small business at $45,000, up from $20,000 in 2015, and one in five small-business liability claims is now a fall.

levers.name: When a storm is forecast

options.label: Open as usual with the full schedule
Open with whoever lives close; cancel the other shifts the night before
Close on warning days and tell staff the evening before

levers.note: Applies only on days with a National Weather Service warning (blizzard, winter storm, flash flood, tropical storm). open_as_usual: full wages against 40% of normal traffic, and workers who cannot get in are simply absent. skeleton_crew: wages for half the staff; shifts cancelled the night before cost nothing. close_for_the_day: no sales and no wages if staff were told before they reported; anyone who already reported is owed call-in pay of 3 hours at the minimum wage (12 NYCRR §146-1.5; the State Labor Department applies it to weather closings). The effects written here are month-level placeholders: 1-2 warning days a month in winter. The shortcut storm_day_no_call_in_pay is the illegal variant.

levers.name: Your stretch of sidewalk

options.label: Sweep at opening and before closing, out to 18 inches into the street
options.note: D11: was $85. D07 valued 10 minutes a day of a barista ($85). Staff hours are already paid in staff.hoursPerMonth, so charging it again counts the same hour twice. Power washing stays a real extra ($150 a visit, D07).

options.label: Sweep twice a day and power-wash once a month
options.note: D11: was $235. D07 valued 10 minutes a day of a barista ($85). Staff hours are already paid in staff.hoursPerMonth, so charging it again counts the same hour twice. Power washing stays a real extra ($150 a visit, D07).

options.label: It is the city's sidewalk

levers.note: Sweeping: 10 minutes a day of a $17.00 worker x 30 days = $85. Power wash: $150 a visit is my planning value for a 20-foot storefront; no New York price list was found. The duty is real: DSNY makes owners and tenants clean the sidewalk and the gutter 18 inches into the street, even when someone else dropped the litter.

levers.name: A sidewalk shed over your door

options.label: Wait for it to come down
Hang a temporary sign on the shed and light your entrance
Lawyer letter for a rent credit; report idle months to 311

levers.note: Only shown while a shed covers the storefront. Sign: the Buildings Department lets a business whose lawful sign is blocked put a temporary sign on the face of the shed directly in front of the storefront; $150 a month = a $1,200 banner and LED strip written off over 8 months (planning value). The +3% recovers about half of the measured loss (3.5-9.7% of weekly transactions). Rent credit: nothing in the law gives a tenant a credit for a shed; it is whatever the lease says. -5% of rent for a $250-a-month lawyer retainer is my estimate of a negotiated outcome, not a right. Local Law 48 of 2025 fines the building owner for months with no work, which is the tenant's leverage.

levers.name: When the street is torn up or the train is out

options.label: Change nothing
'We are open' signs at both corners, a punch card for regulars
Push pickup orders and delivery while the block is hard to reach

levers.note: Only shown during a street, subway or utility disruption. The city pays nothing for lost sales (Small Business Services FAQ, 2022), so the owner pays for any mitigation. $200 = printed signs and a 10th-drink-free card at about 1% of sales; +3% is my estimate of what it wins back out of a 10-22% loss. Delivery: $100 of listing promotion; delivery orders also pay the platform commission that the pack models elsewhere.

levers.name: Parade, fair or race on your street

options.label: A normal day
Extra barista, double pastry order, cups stocked the night before
Sell five fast items from the door, no seating

levers.note: Applies on announced event days only. $120 = one extra 7-hour shift at $17.00. Deliveries cannot reach a closed street, so stock arrives the day before. The capacity gains are month-level placeholders; on the day itself the window menu roughly doubles orders per hour (design value). The crowd is only worth what you can serve.

levers.name: Basement and heavy rain

options.label: Stock on the basement floor, standard insurance
Stock on racks 6 inches up, water-backup rider on the policy, door dam for flood warnings
Backwater valve on the sewer line, sump pump, flood policy

levers.note: basic: water-backup endorsement $50-$250 a year on consumer policies ($15 a month at the middle; no commercial quote was found) + four dunnage racks and a door barrier, about $480 over two years = $20. full: backwater valve installed for about $3,000 and a sump pump for $1,500, written off over five years = $75, plus a commercial flood policy at a planning value of $1,400 a year = $115. A standard business owner's policy covers neither flood nor sewer backup. The lever decides how much the flash_flood_warning and sewer_backup events cost: none = full loss, basic = stock saved and cleanup insured, full = no water.

levers.name: Smoke days

options.label: Nothing special
High-grade filter in the air handler, a portable air cleaner, masks for staff

levers.note: $40 = a MERV-13 filter changed quarterly, a $300 HEPA unit over three years and a box of KN95 masks (planning value). On a smoke day the option keeps the room usable: the shop loses street traffic but not the customers already inside, and staff are not sent home. Effects are applied by the wildfire_smoke_day event.

levers.name: Keeping rodents out

options.label: Rely on the exterminator
Door sweeps, sealed pipe gaps, rodent-proof bins, trash out of the shop every night

levers.note: $60 = $700 of door sweeps, steel wool, sealant and two steel bins over two years, plus ten minutes of closing labor a day. Works with the existing pest_control lever: an exterminator treats, sealing keeps them out. It decides whether the seasonal pressure events (construction next door, summer peak, first cold week) turn into the existing pest_activity violation.

levers.name: Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year's Day

options.label: Closed on the three big holidays
Open 8 to 2 with volunteers at time-and-a-half
Open all day at regular pay

levers.note: New York has no rule that makes a private employer pay a premium for work on a holiday; holiday pay exists only where a contract or the shop's own policy promises it (law-firm guide; the State Labor Department text was not opened). Time-and-a-half is a custom, and the price of keeping a crew: $110 = two baristas x 6 hours x $8.50 premium, once in the month. A holiday morning on a residential block is one of the busiest of the year because everything else is closed; in an office district it is dead. +1% of the month is my estimate for one strong day. Regular pay on Christmas costs goodwill: the quality effect is a design value that should feed turnover in D05.

levers.name: If the power goes out

options.label: Nothing prepared
Fridge thermometers and a log, ice chests, battery lights, card reader that works offline, claim form ready

levers.note: $15 a month = about $350 of coolers, thermometers and lanterns over two years (planning value). With basic, an outage of up to 8 hours loses no stock and the shop can sell batch coffee and pastries for cash or offline card; with none, milk above 41°F for more than two hours is discarded (the existing spoiled_food rule) and the Con Edison claim fails for lack of an itemized list. D03 owns generators and equipment protection.

levers.name: Sidewalk cellar doors during deliveries

options.label: Cones out and one person stays at the open hatch
options.note: D11: was $45. The spotter is a barista already on shift (D07 valued 10 minutes x 16 days = $45); charging it again counts the same paid hours twice.

options.label: Open the doors and carry on

levers.note: Only for places with a sidewalk hatch. $45 = 10 minutes of a second worker on 16 delivery days. Practitioner summaries of the Administrative Code: when cellar doors are open someone must stay there to steer people around the opening; doors must sit flush and bear weight. A fall is a claim under §7-210, the same route as the icy sidewalk.

levers.name: After closing

options.label: Lock the door, leave the float in the till
Monitored alarm, camera, cash out of the till every night

levers.note: $55 = alarm monitoring at about $40 and a camera subscription at $15 (planning values; a roll-down gate, where the landlord allows one, is a setup cost for D03). Burglary and theft are 20% of small-business claims in The Hartford's 2025 review. The option decides the break_in event.

levers.name: Music

options.label: Licensed background music service for businesses
Your own playlists with ASCAP, BMI and SESAC licenses
No music
Your personal streaming account on the shop speakers

levers.note: Vendor guides for 2026: ASCAP from $324-$502 a year, BMI from about $312-$415, SESAC from $580: $636 to $1,600 a year for a small cafe, here $110 a month for all three. Business music services that include the licenses advertise roughly $17 to $50 a month; $35 is my midpoint. Quality effects are design values.

levers.name: Practice inspections

options.label: None: the first inspector you meet is the real one
One city consultative inspection a year
Private food safety consultant every quarter

levers.note: Seen at NYC Health: a consultative inspection costs $400 for a restaurant that has already been graded ($100 once for a new one before its first graded inspection); it produces no violations unless a public health hazard cannot be fixed on the spot. $400 / 12 = $33, rounded to $35. The private consultant at about $350 a visit, four visits a year, is my estimate. In the proposed inspection model (extra.mechanics.inspection_score_and_grade) a practice inspection removes the general violations a new owner does not know about.

levers.name: Handling pastries and garnishes

options.label: Tongs, tissue and gloves for anything ready to eat
Bare hands, faster line

levers.note: $40 a month of deli tissue and gloves is my estimate from restaurant-supply prices. The violation and its fine are in violations.bare_hand_contact.

levers.name: When someone says they are an inspector

options.label: Staff check the photo ID and badge, call you, and let the inspector work
Staff say the owner is out and keep them waiting
Staff do whatever anyone with a clipboard says, cash included

levers.note: A standing instruction, free either way. The first option also defeats impostors (extra.eventCatalog.fake_inspector_visit): real inspectors never take payment on the spot; fines are paid to the city after a hearing. The third option has no violation; it loses money to scams.

levers.name: When a worker complains about pay or safety

options.label: Hear it, check the records, fix what is wrong
Cut their shifts until they quit

levers.note: A standing instruction. Punishing a complaint turns one wage question into a second, bigger case (violations.retaliation_firing).

levers.name: Legal help

options.label: Handle summonses and letters yourself
Hospitality lawyer on call and a representative for city hearings

levers.note: $150 a month is my estimate of a small retainer; no public price list exists. In the proposed hearing model (extra.mechanics.oath_hearing_choices) representation means no missed hearings and the mitigated penalty wherever the schedule offers one. OATH's own Help Center is free.

levers.name: Labels on food you pack yourself

options.label: Printed label with ingredients and major allergens on every wrapped item
A sticker with the name, nothing else

levers.note: Public Health Law §1357, in force since November 12, 2026: food prepared, packed and sold on the same premises must carry a label that names its major allergens. $30 a month for a label printer's rolls is my estimate. The law itself sets no penalty; the game charges the allergy-notice violation, and the larger exposure is the allergic-reaction claim in extra.lawsuits.

levers.name: Card payouts

options.label: Free next-business-day transfers
Instant transfers, 1.95% of every dollar moved

levers.note: Seen at Square: standard transfers are free and arrive the next business day for sales taken before 5 PM Pacific; none are sent on Saturday, so Friday-Sunday sales land on Monday, or Tuesday when Monday is a bank holiday. Instant and same-day transfers cost 1.95% of the amount. If every card dollar is moved instantly: 1.95% x ($51,000 x 90% x 1.08875 + $2,000 of card tips) = $1,010 a month. The honest use is a few transfers a year, about $20 per $1,000 moved.

levers.name: Sales tax and payroll tax money

options.label: Sweep tax money into a separate account every day
Leave it in the operating account

levers.note: No cost either way. With one account the bank balance looks $13,600 richer just before each sales tax date (3 x $51,000 x 8.875%) and the payroll taxes withheld for the month sit there too. The engine should show "cash that is yours" separately when the first option is on, and only the raw balance when the second is on. Spending the money and not paying is the shortcut keep_sales_tax or spend_payroll_withholding.

levers.name: Owner's estimated income tax

options.label: Pay every quarter: April 15, June 15, September 15, January 15
Keep the cash in the shop and pay it all next April, with interest

levers.note: IRS, fourth quarter of 2026: the underpayment rate is 7% a year, compounded daily. Paying late is not a violation: the IRS adds interest for the days each instalment was short. No interest at all is due if the instalments cover 100% of last year's tax (110% when last year's income was over $150,000), which a first-year owner who was an employee last year often already meets through a spouse's or own withholding. Planning cost: the reference owner owes $36,300 a year (extra.referenceMonth: $3,026 a month); each instalment is on average about 7.5 months late: $36,300 x 7% x 7.5 / 12 = $1,590 a year = $130 a month. New York State charges its own interest on its part; the state rate was not found. The real risk is not the interest: it is arriving in April without the money.

levers.name: Owner's health insurance

options.label: Stay on a spouse's employer plan
Marketplace silver plan for yourself
Marketplace silver plan for a family of four

levers.note: $806.61 is the 2026 lowest cost silver plan in Bronx, Kings and Queens counties (NY State of Health). The family figure is that premium x 2.85, the family tier factor I remember for New York's community-rated market; the factor was not verified this session. Before subsidies: for 2026 a family of four with income of $112,525-$128,600 qualifies only for reduced cost sharing (seen in the marketplace's 2026 plan card). Health insurance for New York-area service firms rose 12.9% in a year (Manhattan Chamber of Commerce, October 2026).

levers.name: When cash is short: who waits

options.label: Pay everyone on the due date
Pay rent on the 10th and take the late fee
options.consequence: after three late months in a row the landlord sends a default notice; under a good guy guarantee the owner is then no longer a "good guy"

options.label: Stretch supplier invoices by two weeks
options.consequence: after two stretched months the roaster and the dairy move the account to cash on delivery

levers.note: Both are legal and both are what owners actually do first. The late fee is a planning value: 5% of a $6,000 rent, a common clause in New York shop leases (not a statute; read the lease). Stretching suppliers frees about two weeks of purchases once, roughly $6,600 at the reference cost of goods of $13,260 a month, and costs the open account. Neither is allowed for tax money or wages: those are the shortcuts.

levers.name: Repair and slow-season reserve

options.label: Nothing set aside
Set aside 1% of sales
Set aside 3% of sales

levers.note: Not an expense: the money moves to a reserve the business still owns (see mechanic reserve_fund). Amounts are 1% and 3% of the reference month's $51,000 of sales. One-off bills (repairs, audit, tax escalation, claims) are paid from the reserve first.

levers.name: Second keyholder and second certificate

options.label: Only you hold the keys and the Food Protection Certificate
Train a lead: second certificate, keys, opening and closing

levers.note: $160 a month = a $1 an hour lead premium x 140 hours + the $24 exam and about 15 paid study hours ($255) spread over a year. Protects against flu_takes_the_only_supervisor and softens key_barista_leaves and owner_burnout.

levers.name: Sign on the sidewalk

options.label: Window and wall sign only
Chalkboard A-frame on the sidewalk

levers.note: +2% demand is a game-balance value. Sanitation fines: $100 first, up to $300 after (figures reported in 2015).

levers.name: Gift cards

options.label: No gift cards
Promote gift cards in December

levers.note: Moves cash from January-February into December; see gift_card_hangover.

levers.name: Complaints and refunds

options.label: Remake or refund without argument
options.note: D11: was $250. D10 put remade drinks at about 0.5% of sales ($250) valued at the menu price. A remake costs the shop its ingredients and cup, not the price: 0.5% x $50,000 x 0.26 (unit.cogsPerUnit / unit.refPrice = 2.21 / 8.50) = $65.

options.label: No refunds

levers.note: $250 a month = about 0.5% of sales in remade drinks, my estimate.

shortcuts.name: Run shifts with no certified supervisor
shortcuts.what: A Food Protection Certificate holder must be on site every hour you are open. Covering every shift means training more people and paying leads; skipping it saves about $120 a month. Each inspection that finds nobody certified costs $400 and 10 points.
shortcuts.note: My estimate: certifying and paying a lead on every shift costs about $120 a month more (the exam is $24 a person; a lead earns about $6 an hour more than a barista: NY DOL OEWS Q1 2026, NYC supervisors median $24.07 vs counter workers $17.57). The fine is $400 and 10 points (Appendix 23-C, 04A).

shortcuts.name: Sell yesterday's milk and pastries
shortcuts.what: Nothing gets thrown out: old pastries go back in the case, milk sits on the counter. Saves about 1% of sales in waste. Spoiled or warm food is a public health hazard: $250-$600 per citation and a fast road to a C grade.
shortcuts.note: My estimate: about 1% of sales is food thrown out at the end of the day. The fine for cold food above 41°F or food not protected is $250-$600 (Appendix 23-C, 02G and 04H).

shortcuts.name: Sell pastries baked at home
shortcuts.what: Baking at home instead of buying from a licensed bakery cuts pastry cost by more than half, about 3% of sales. Food from a home kitchen is food from an unapproved source: $400-$600 and a public health hazard on your record.
shortcuts.note: My estimate: pastry is about 6% of sales and home baking halves its cost = about 3% of sales. Home-cooked food is "food from an unapproved source": $400-$600 (Appendix 23-C, 03A).

shortcuts.name: Keep part of the tips
shortcuts.what: The owner takes a cut of the tip jar and the card tips: about $150 per barista a month. Tips belong to the staff by law. A wage claim returns every dollar double and reaches back six years.
shortcuts.note: My estimate: about $150 a month per barista out of tips. Labor Law §196-d forbids any part of the gratuities to the employer; §198(1-a) adds 100% liquidated damages (texts seen at nysenate.gov).

shortcuts.name: Unpaid trial shifts and training
shortcuts.what: New hires work a few shifts "on trial" and train for free: about $85 per worker a month. Every hour worked must be paid at $17.00 or more; unpaid hours are owed back double.
shortcuts.note: My arithmetic: about 5 unpaid hours per worker a month x $17.00 NYC minimum = $85 (NY DOL, minimum unchanged on January 1, 2027).

shortcuts.name: Long days without the extra hour
shortcuts.what: Open-to-close and split shifts stretch a workday past 10 hours. The law adds one extra hour of pay at $17.00 for each such day; skipping it saves about $135 per worker a month and is owed back double.
shortcuts.note: My arithmetic: about 8 days a month with a workday spread over 10 hours x one extra hour at $17.00 = $136 per worker (12 NYCRR §146-1.6; the minimum seen at NY DOL).

shortcuts.name: Put tables on the sidewalk without a license
shortcuts.what: A few tables outside bring about 2% more sales, and you skip the $1,050 license, the $1,500 deposit and a wait that often runs past a year. The city fines $500, then $1,000 each time, and can order the tables removed.
shortcuts.note: My estimate: a few tables outside add about 2% of sales. Unlicensed outdoor dining is fined $500, then $1,000, with no warning (Dining Out NYC enforcement page, seen).

shortcuts.name: Skip grease interceptor cleaning
shortcuts.what: Milk fat and coffee grounds fill the grease interceptor under the sink. Skipping the pump-out saves about $75 a month. Inspectors measure it: more than 25% full means a fine of $100 to $1,500, and a backup floods your floor.
shortcuts.note: My estimate: about one pump-out a quarter at $200-$330 (vendor and consumer cost guides seen through search; a Manhattan average of $329-$473 per service) = about $75 a month. Fine $100-$1,500 (NYC Business restaurant page, DEP).

shortcuts.name: Renovate without a Buildings permit
shortcuts.what: A handyman moves the sink, adds outlets and a wall over a weekend: no architect, no filing, no waiting. One neighbor's 311 call brings a Stop Work Order and a penalty of 21 times the permit fee, $6,000 at the least, and you file the plans anyway.
shortcuts.note: A one-time decision during build-out: it saves the architect, expediter and filing fees (the pack's $7,000 line) and the weeks of waiting. Shown here as $600 a month for 12 months until the engine supports one-time shortcuts.

shortcuts.name: Keep building under a Stop Work Order
shortcuts.what: Every month the order hangs on the door is a month of rent with no sales, so the crew works at night. Saves a month of rent each month. Working through the order is $6,000 each time it is caught, and a crime.

shortcuts.name: Let a handyman do the plumbing and wiring
shortcuts.what: A licensed plumber and electrician quote twice what the handyman does. Unlicensed work cannot be filed or inspected: if anyone looks, it is torn out and redone by a licensed firm, with a fine on top.

shortcuts.name: Keep trading on the seller's Health permit
shortcuts.what: You bought the shop on Friday and want to sell coffee on Monday. The seller's permit died with the sale: permits cannot be transferred. Until yours is issued, or 22 days after you applied, you are running a restaurant with no permit.

shortcuts.name: Close the purchase without the bulk-sale notice
shortcuts.what: The seller wants the money this week and the notice to the Tax Department adds at least 10 days, maybe 90. Skip it and every dollar of sales tax the seller never paid becomes your personal debt, up to the price you paid.

shortcuts.name: Open in a space that is not legal for a cafe
shortcuts.what: The rent is low because the Certificate of Occupancy says "store", or there is none. Legalizing the use takes a letter from the Buildings Department or an amended certificate filed by the owner. Open anyway and the fine runs from $400 to $25,000.

shortcuts.name: Add chairs past the 19-seat line without a customer restroom
shortcuts.what: A few more chairs lift seated sales by about 3%, and you skip a $12,000 restroom. With 20 or more seats, outdoor ones included, and no toilet for customers the Health Department writes a critical violation: $300 and 10 points at each inspection, and the fix is still owed.

shortcuts.name: Stop restocking and checking the restroom
shortcuts.what: Nobody checks the paper, the bin or the door closer during the shift: about $60 a month of supplies and time saved. A toilet not maintained or supplied costs $200 and 2 to 5 points at inspection.

shortcuts.name: Hang the big sign without a permit
shortcuts.what: A sign over 6 square feet needs a permit and a licensed sign hanger: about $1,500 and a month of waiting. A friend with a ladder does it Saturday. If someone reports the block's signs to 311, the fine starts at $6,000.
shortcuts.note: A one-time decision: the $1,500 for the filing and the licensed sign hanger is my estimate; shown as $125 a month for 12 months until the engine supports one-time shortcuts.

shortcuts.name: A-frame sign in the middle of the sidewalk
shortcuts.what: A chalkboard out by the curb catches people from both directions: about 1% more sales. A sign may not stand more than 3 feet from your wall; farther out it is an obstruction: $100, then up to $300.
shortcuts.note: The 1% is my estimate; no measurement of A-frame signs on sales was found.

shortcuts.name: Stack deliveries in the back exit
shortcuts.what: No storage room, so milk crates and cup cases live in the rear corridor. Saves about $150 a month of off-site storage or lost seats. A blocked exit is $950, or $475 if cleared before the hearing, and the first thing a fire officer looks at.
shortcuts.note: The $150 is my estimate of a small self-storage unit in the outer boroughs.

shortcuts.name: Skip the yearly backflow test
shortcuts.what: The valve on your water line must be tested every year by a certified tester, about $240 a visit. Skip it and save $20 a month. The city knows from its own records which reports are missing: $500, or $50 if you file before the hearing.
shortcuts.note: The $240 price of a test is my estimate from plumbers' advertised ranges ($150-$350); no official price exists.

shortcuts.name: Pack the room on event nights
shortcuts.what: Open mic, launch party, 90 people in a room approved for far fewer: about 2% more sales a month. Overcrowding is $950 the first time and $2,375 the second, and the fire officer can empty the room mid-event.
shortcuts.note: The 2% is my estimate: two packed evenings a month at double the usual evening sales.

shortcuts.name: Put customer tables in the cellar
shortcuts.what: The cellar is free space: tables down there add about 3% to sales. A cellar approved for storage is not approved for customers: occupancy contrary to the Certificate of Occupancy costs $1,250, or $6,250 if you miss the hearing, and the tables have to go.

shortcuts.name: Turn the music up for evening events under apartments
shortcuts.what: A loud room keeps an evening crowd: about 1% more sales. Music from a business may not pass 42 decibels inside a neighbor's home. The first violation is $2,000, cut to $0 only if you prove you fixed it.

shortcuts.name: Add tables beyond your licensed outdoor area
shortcuts.what: Two more tables past the line on your site plan add about 1% to sales in season. The first time the city sends a corrective action request and gives you 30 days; after that it is $200, then $500 each time, and repeat offenders can lose the license.

shortcuts.name: Keep the milk after a warm night
shortcuts.what: The fridge failed or the power was out, and the milk sat above 41°F for more than 2 hours. The rule says throw it out; keeping it saves about $50 a month on average. Warm or spoiled food is a public health hazard: $250-$600 and 7 to 28 points.

shortcuts.name: Let the extinguisher tags expire
shortcuts.what: Two extinguishers need a certified company once a year, about $120, and a signed check every month. Skipping saves $10 a month. A fire inspector reads the tag first: $600, or $300 if fixed before the hearing.
shortcuts.note: The $120 a year for two units is my estimate from service companies' advertised prices; no official price exists.

shortcuts.name: Let a handyman plumb and wire new equipment
shortcuts.what: A licensed plumber or electrician with a Buildings Department permit costs about $125 a month more over a year of installs and replacements. Work without a permit costs 21 times the permit fee, at least $6,000, even if you rip it out afterwards.

shortcuts.name: Keep a failing fridge in service
shortcuts.what: The reach-in no longer holds 41°F on hot afternoons. Putting off a new one saves about $219 a month. Equipment that cannot keep food cold is a critical violation, $300-$350, and the warm milk in it is a second one.

shortcuts.name: Put off the water heater repair
shortcuts.what: The heater is dying and the hand sink runs lukewarm. A plumber costs money today; waiting saves about $120 a month. No hot water at the hand sink is 10 points, 28 if the whole shop is without it, and the inspector can close you until it is fixed.
shortcuts.note: My estimate: a $1,400 repair or replacement put off for a year.

shortcuts.name: Drain the ice machine into a bucket
shortcuts.what: A proper drain line with an air gap means a plumber. Letting the ice machine and the fridge drip into a bucket saves about $56 a month. Inspectors cite it as improper drainage, and standing water breeds drain flies.

shortcuts.name: Buy foam cups
shortcuts.what: Foam hot cups cost about a cent and a half less than paper and need no sleeve: about 0.2% of sales. Foam cups and containers have been banned in New York City since 2019: $150, then $250, then $500.
shortcuts.note: 1.5 cents saved per $8.50 order = 0.18% of sales; cup prices from the pack's supplies line.

shortcuts.name: Plastic stirrers and a straw in every cold cup
shortcuts.what: Plastic stirrers and unwrapped plastic straws are the cheapest on the shelf and save a few seconds per drink: about $40 a month. Plastic stirrers are banned and plastic straws are on request only: $100, then $200, then $400.

shortcuts.name: Cancel the private carter and take the trash home
shortcuts.what: No carter contract: about $250 a month saved. Every business must have an authorized private carter; the city does not collect business trash, and in a waste zone you get assigned a carter at the maximum rate anyway.

shortcuts.name: No carter: use the corner baskets
shortcuts.what: Cancel the private carter and drop the shop's bags in public litter baskets or the building's residential pile: saves about $250 a month. Agents open the bags and find your receipts: $100 to $300 each time.

shortcuts.name: One bag for everything
shortcuts.what: No sorting, no second bin, no cardboard to flatten: about $40 a month of staff time and service. Every business must separate recyclables: $100, then $200, then $400.

shortcuts.name: Buy everything tax-free on the resale certificate
shortcuts.what: Show the resale certificate for napkins, stirrers, cleaning chemicals and small equipment as well as cups: about $55 a month of sales tax not paid. An audit bills the tax, the same amount again as a penalty, and $50 per invoice.

shortcuts.name: Sell CBD lattes
shortcuts.what: A CBD shot adds $3 to a drink and a line on the chalkboard: about 1% more sales. The Health Department treats CBD in food and drinks as an unapproved additive: the product is embargoed and the fine runs $200 to $650.
shortcuts.note: The 1% is my estimate: a $3 add-on in one of every 35 orders.

shortcuts.name: Keep the premium words, pour the cheap stuff
shortcuts.what: The menu still says single-origin, organic milk and Oatly; the bar pours a commodity blend and the cheapest cartons. Saves about 3% of sales. Each false claim is a separate deceptive practice: $525 and up, $3,500 if you knew.

shortcuts.name: Keep selling a recalled product
shortcuts.what: The recall notice names lots that are on your shelf. Pulling them means a write-off of about $150 and a day without the item. Selling recalled food is selling adulterated food: a summons of up to $1,200, and a lawsuit if anyone gets sick.

shortcuts.name: Bottle cold brew for the deli next door
shortcuts.what: Thirty bottles a day to two neighboring shops adds about 2% to sales. Your city permit covers only your own counter: selling bottled drinks to other stores needs a state food processing license. Up to $600, then $1,200, and each day counts.

shortcuts.name: Pay baristas every two weeks instead of every week
shortcuts.what: Half the payroll runs and a week of wages stays in your account a little longer: about $30 a month. Baristas are manual workers and must be paid weekly. A first finding costs interest; a repeat costs damages equal to all the wages paid late.

shortcuts.name: Hire on a handshake: no pay notice, no pay stubs
shortcuts.what: No forms, no stubs, start tomorrow: saves about $12 per worker a month. A worker who never got a pay notice can claim $50 a work day, and $250 a work day for missing pay stubs, up to $5,000 each.

shortcuts.name: Send staff home on slow days, pay only minutes worked
shortcuts.what: Rain kills the afternoon, so you cut the shift after an hour: about $68 per worker a month. Anyone who reports for a shift is owed at least 3 hours of pay. Unpaid call-in pay is owed back double.

shortcuts.name: One person per shift, no meal break
shortcuts.what: You never schedule a second person to give breaks: about $630 a month. A shift of more than 6 hours across lunchtime carries a 30-minute meal period, and a worker who asks for an uninterrupted one must get it.

shortcuts.name: Take register shortages out of staff pay
shortcuts.what: When the drawer is short or a customer walks out, the barista on shift covers it: about $13 per worker a month. New York forbids deducting shortages, breakage or spoilage from wages, even when one person had the drawer. Owed back double.

shortcuts.name: Staff buy the logo shirts and wash them at home
shortcuts.what: You require the branded shirt and apron but supply none: about $91 per worker a month. The employer must pay for a required uniform and, unless it supplies enough wash-and-wear sets, $21.10 a week to keep it clean.

shortcuts.name: Give the manager a share of the tips
shortcuts.what: A fifth share of the tip pool, about $400 a month, tops up the manager instead of your payroll. Managers and owners may not take any part of staff tips. The tips are owed back double, plus a federal penalty.

shortcuts.name: Pay the $11.35 tipped wage with no notice or tip records
shortcuts.what: You count $5.65 an hour of tips toward the wage: about $904 per worker a month. The credit is legal only with a written notice, tip records, and tips that really cover it. Without them the full $17.00 was due all along, doubled.

shortcuts.name: Flat weekly salary for the shift lead, 50-hour weeks
shortcuts.what: $1,100 a week instead of $1,320 on the clock: about $950 a month. Under $1,275 a week nobody is exempt from overtime, and restaurant staff must be paid by the hour. The back pay is figured on $27.50 an hour, then doubled.

shortcuts.name: Cut the hours of the worker who asked about pay
shortcuts.what: The questions stop and you skip about $150 a month of corrections. Punishing a worker for a wage complaint, even a mistaken one, is a separate violation: a penalty of $1,000 to $10,000, lost pay, and up to $20,000 in damages.

shortcuts.name: Hire 16-year-olds with no working papers and let them close
shortcuts.what: A high-school student takes $17 where a trained barista wants $21: about $320 a month. Under 18 means working papers, 4 hours on a school night and no work after 10 pm without written consent. Fines now reach $10,000 for a first violation.

shortcuts.name: Friends and family work the counter for free
shortcuts.what: Ten unpaid hours a week on the register saves about $760 a month. A for-profit shop cannot have volunteers: they are employees owed the minimum wage, doubled, and they are not covered if they get burned.

shortcuts.name: Split the cash jar at closing and report nothing
shortcuts.what: Cash tips never touch payroll, so you skip your 7.65% on them: about 0.15% of sales. The IRS can bill your share later, and since 2025 staff lose their tax deduction on any tip that is not reported.

shortcuts.name: Fire the baristas who started a union petition
shortcuts.what: The petition dies and you avoid a raise worth about $240 per worker a month. Firing someone for organizing is an unfair labor practice: the labor board orders them rehired with full back pay and interest.

shortcuts.name: Skip the disability and Paid Family Leave policy
shortcuts.what: No policy, no paperwork: saves about $3 per worker a month. It is mandatory from the first employee: a misdemeanor, a penalty of up to 0.5% of payroll plus $500, and you pay any claim yourself or 1% of payroll, whichever is more.

shortcuts.name: Buy a batch of five-star reviews
shortcuts.what: A 'reputation' seller posts glowing reviews for less than honest marketing costs. Platforms flag it publicly and the FTC's review rule allows up to $53,088 per fake review.

shortcuts.name: Free cookie for a five-star review
shortcuts.what: Trading a freebie for a positive review looks harmless. The FTC rule bans rewards that depend on what the review says, and Yelp demotes businesses caught asking.

shortcuts.name: Take down the B
shortcuts.what: A B or C card in the window scares off walk-ins. Leave the old A up, or 'lose' the new card, and keep about 3% of sales. The card has a serial number and inspectors and neighbors check: $500-$1,000 for no card, $1,000-$2,000 for removing or faking it.
shortcuts.note: The 3% is my estimate. Evidence of direction and size: a study of more than 15,000 NYC restaurants over 28 months found A grades raise revenue and lower the chance of closing, and C grades lower revenue compared with B (Silver, Rothbart and others, Public Administration Review, 2019); a Los Angeles sales-tax analysis put an A at up to +6% and a B at +1-2%, a gap of about 4 points.

shortcuts.name: Add a card fee at the register
shortcuts.what: A 3.5% fee appears on the card reader, not on the menu: it wipes out your card costs, about 3% of sales. The law allows a credit card surcharge only if the full card price is posted and it is no more than your real cost: up to $500 per violation.
shortcuts.note: 3.5% on the 90% of sales paid by card (the pack's card model) = 3.15% of sales.

shortcuts.name: Tape flyers to lamp posts and parked cars
shortcuts.what: Cheaper than ads. Every flyer on a pole, street furniture or a car is its own violation: $75 to $150 the first time, $150 to $250 after, plus the cost of removal.

shortcuts.name: Dogs welcome inside
shortcuts.what: Dog owners become regulars: about 1% more sales. A pet inside a food shop is a critical violation: $200 to $350 and 5 or more points toward your grade. Only service animals may come in; pets may sit at outdoor tables if you post the sign.
shortcuts.note: The 1% is my estimate.

shortcuts.name: Do not clear the snow
shortcuts.what: Nobody shovels or salts your sidewalk after a snowfall. You save the labor. A sanitation agent can ticket you the same day, and if someone falls on your ice the claim follows you for three years.

shortcuts.name: Trash bags on the curb, no bins
shortcuts.what: Bags go out at closing with no lidded bin, or the bins stay out all morning. Saves the bins and a few minutes a day, about $20 a month. $50 the first time, $100 the second, $200 every time after, and bags on the curb feed the rats that cost you points.
shortcuts.note: My estimate: two 44-gallon lidded bins at about $120 each, replaced every year.

shortcuts.name: Door propped open with the air conditioning on
shortcuts.what: An open door and a wave of cold air pull people in off a hot sidewalk. It is illegal for every store in the city, and it adds to your electric bill.

shortcuts.name: Speaker at the open door
shortcuts.what: Music out onto the sidewalk pulls people in: about 1% more sales. The people upstairs call 311; a reading over 42 decibels inside their apartment costs $2,000, then $4,000, then $6,000.
shortcuts.note: The 1% is my estimate.

shortcuts.name: Candles on the tables, no permit
shortcuts.what: Candles make the evening. The FDNY open flame permit costs $210 a year; skipping it saves $18 a month. Open flame without the permit: $700, or $350 if you get the permit before the hearing.

shortcuts.name: Stop sweeping the sidewalk
shortcuts.what: Nobody sweeps the sidewalk and the 18 inches of gutter in front of the shop: about 15 minutes a day, $85 a month. Sanitation agents ticket during two posted hours a day: $100 to $300 each, sidewalk and gutter separately.
shortcuts.note: 15 minutes a day x 30 days x $17.00 an hour = $127; I count two thirds of it because some sweeping happens anyway.

shortcuts.name: Leave the step at the door
shortcuts.what: A portable ramp, a bell, a lower counter section and a website a screen reader can use cost about $2,400. Skipping them saves $100 a month. Lawyers file thousands of these suits a year in New York, and settling one costs about $10,000 plus the fixes.
shortcuts.note: My estimate: $2,400 of readily achievable fixes spread over 24 months. A small business gets half of such spending back as a federal tax credit of up to $5,000 a year (IRS Form 8826).

shortcuts.name: Skip the harassment policy and training
shortcuts.what: No written policy, no yearly training: saves an hour of paid time per worker a year and some paperwork, about $5 per worker a month. The state requires both from every employer; without them you have no defense when a claim comes.
shortcuts.note: One paid hour at $17-$21 a year per worker plus the owner's time, rounded up to $5 a month; the state's model policy and training are free.

shortcuts.name: Let the health permit lapse
shortcuts.what: The Food Service Establishment Permit renews every year for $280. Forgetting or skipping it saves $23 a month. Serving without a current permit is $1,000, $2,000 if you ignore the summons, and grounds to close the shop the same day.
shortcuts.note: $280 / 12 = $23. In life this is almost always forgetfulness, not a plan: the renewal notice goes to an old email address.

shortcuts.name: Use the withheld payroll taxes to pay the rent
shortcuts.what: You run payroll properly but do not send the IRS and the state what you withheld: about 23% of payroll stays in the bank. That money is held in trust. The IRS adds 2%-15% and can charge the whole amount to you personally, LLC or not.

shortcuts.name: Add a 4% "wellness fee" to every check
shortcuts.what: Menu prices stay the same and a 4% fee line is added at the end. New York City restaurants may not add a surcharge on top of listed prices; a real service charge must be disclosed before the customer orders. Inspectors check receipts against the menu.

shortcuts.name: Ring lattes up as tax-free groceries
shortcuts.what: The register is set so a tenth of taxable drinks ring as exempt "beans to go": you keep 8.875% on those sales, about 0.9% of all sales. An auditor rebuilds your sales from cups and milk bought: tax back, up to 30% penalty, interest.

shortcuts.name: Tell the workers' comp insurer half your payroll
shortcuts.what: Premium is charged per $100 of payroll, so reporting half of it halves the bill: about 1% of payroll. The yearly premium audit asks for your payroll tax returns. Concealing payroll counts as having no coverage: up to $2,000 per 10 days.

shortcuts.name: Play your own streaming playlist
shortcuts.what: A personal music account is not licensed for a shop. Saves the business plan fee until a rights society notices.

shortcuts.name: Seat customers in the back yard
shortcuts.what: Twelve more seats without a filing at the Buildings Department. One complaint from a neighbor ends it.

shortcuts.name: Stay open while the water is off
shortcuts.what: No running water means no handwashing and no dishwashing. Closing for the day costs a day of sales.

shortcuts.name: Start the build-out before the Buildings permit is issued
shortcuts.what: Your contractor starts now instead of waiting about 20 days for DOB approval. If an inspector or a neighbor's 311 call catches it, work stops and you pay a penalty.
shortcuts.note: One-time, during setup only: the doors open extra.preOpening.dobPermitDays (20) days sooner. Without free rent that is 20 days of rent with no sales, 20 / 30 = 0.67 of a month's rent; inside free rent the gain is 20 more days of sales instead. The engine should apply it as days, not as a monthly saving (request in the report).

shortcuts.name: Let the morning line pack inside past capacity
shortcuts.what: On cold mornings you let everyone squeeze in instead of lining up outside. Fewer people walk on, but the room holds more than the code allows.
shortcuts.note: The real gain comes from the queue model (extra.floorZones): queue room is counted at the 5 sq ft code floor instead of 8.5, so fewer people stand outside. 0.3% of sales is the placeholder the format needs; in the D14 examples the winter outside-line loss is 0.1-0.3% of daily orders. tier: deep.

violations.note: Pay for actual work is required. Call-in pay has shift-specific exceptions; do not apply a universal minimum attendance payment. The inherited damages multiplier and reputation effect require applicable facts.

violations.law: 12 NYCRR §146-1.6; NY Labor Law §198(1-a)
violations.note: The pay entitlement and possible damages are distinct. The inherited damages multiplier and reputation effect are not universally verified outcomes.

violations.name: Sidewalk tables without a Dining Out NYC license
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §§19-160.1, 19-160.4, 19-160.5(c), 19-160.6; 34 RCNY §§5-10, 5-11 (Dining Out NYC)

violations.name: Grease interceptor not maintained
violations.law: 15 RCNY §19-11 (NYC Department of Environmental Protection sewer use rules)
violations.note: Remove unsupported elapsed-month escalation. The penalty schedule distinguishes offense sequence, appearance and default. The inherited ordinary-offense ceiling is not an all-in liability cap. Conflicting primary-source default presentations require legal resolution before implementation; no default replacement invented.

violations.name: Construction, plumbing or electrical work without a Buildings permit
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §28-105.1, §28-213.1 (civil penalty for work without a permit)

violations.name: Working through a Stop Work Order
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §28-207.2 (stop work orders)
violations.criminal: Violating a Stop Work Order is also a misdemeanor under the Administrative Code (§28-207.2, cited from memory).
violations.note: Seen at the Department of Buildings Stop Work Order page: first offense $6,000. The amount for later offenses was not in the excerpt (from memory it is $12,000); the game charges $6,000 for every month the work goes on. The order stays on the door until the permit exists and the penalties are paid.

violations.name: Plumbing or electrical work by an unlicensed person
violations.law: NYC Admin. Code §28-408.1 (plumbing only by a licensed master plumber), §28-410.1, §27-3017 (electrical work only by a licensed electrician); Local Law 46 of 2017
violations.criminal: Unlicensed plumbing or electrical work is a misdemeanor under Title 28; the work has to be opened up, redone by a licensed firm and inspected.
violations.note: Local Law 46 of 2017 (nyc.gov) sets minimum civil penalties for unlicensed plumbing and fire suppression work; the figures were cut off in the extract. The base is one reported hearing-office case (CityLand, 2022): a plumber working with no licensed master plumber supervising was fined $5,000. The real cost is larger: the utility and DOB will not sign off work that no licensed firm filed, so it is redone. closureDays is my estimate for the redo and re-inspection.

violations.name: Bought a business without notifying the Tax Department (bulk sale)
violations.law: NY Tax Law §1141(c); 20 NYCRR Part 537; Form AU-196.10

violations.name: Running a cafe where the Certificate of Occupancy does not allow one
violations.law: NYC Admin. Code §28-118.3.2 (occupancy contrary to the Certificate of Occupancy or Department of Buildings records)
violations.criminal: The Department of Buildings can order the premises vacated until the use is legalized.

violations.name: No customer toilet with 20 or more seats
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.22(b), §81.22(d); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 05E

violations.name: Restroom not maintained or supplied
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.22(c); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 10A

violations.name: Ventilation missing or in disrepair
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.19(c); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 10D

violations.name: Business sign installed without a permit
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §28-105.1; 1 RCNY §102-01 (Buildings penalty schedule)
violations.note: D11 correction. D02 read the Buildings penalty schedule (28-105.1, Class 2: $1,250, $6,250 on default) and D08 the work-without-permit fee rule (21x the permit fee, at least $6,000). violations.name: Step at the door, no ramp, website a screen reader cannot use
violations.law: Americans with Disabilities Act, Title III (42 U.S.C. §12182); NYC Administrative Code §8-107(4); NY Executive Law §296(2)
violations.note: Not a city fine: a private lawsuit. Seyfarth Shaw counted 8,667 federal ADA Title III lawsuits in 2025, of them 3,117 about websites, with New York the busiest state for website suits (1,021). NY1 reported an East Harlem restaurant sued over an 8-inch step with 43 alleged violations, and plaintiffs who each filed more than 100 suits; each suit asks for about $1,000 in damages plus the plaintiff's legal fees and an order to fix the barrier. The federal law gives no damages, but the city and state human rights laws do, and the loser pays the winner's lawyer. The $10,000 settlement-plus-lawyers figure and the $25,000 cap are my estimate: no public statistic of settlements exists because they are confidential. A complaint to the city Commission on Human Rights can instead end in a civil penalty of up to $125,000 (Administrative Code §8-126, cited from memory).

violations.name: No contract with an authorized private carter
violations.law: NYC Admin Code §16-116; Title 16-B (Commercial Waste Zones, Local Law 199 of 2019)
violations.note: Seen in DSNY's printed summary of rules (2015): $100 for not having a private carter under §16-116(b). DSNY's 2025 Commercial Waste Zone report calls the penalties under §16-116 'relatively low' and asks the Council to raise them, so $100 is the floor, not a 2026 schedule. In a zone that has gone live a business with no contract is assigned a carter at the zone's maximum rate: that is why the game formula adds back everything saved.

violations.name: Business trash in a public litter basket
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-120(e); §16-116 (businesses must use a licensed private carter)
violations.note: DSNY collection and set-out laws for businesses, as quoted by web search: 'Under no circumstances can a merchant dispose of any garbage or recyclable materials in a DSNY litter basket'; $100 first offense, $250 second, $350 third and later. The code presumes that the person whose name appears on garbage found in the basket put it there. Second pass: the OATH hearings data set shows this charge ('Improper disposal, DSNY litter basket, 1st offense') only 7 times since January 1, 2025, with $50 or $130 imposed or the case dismissed, so it is rarely ticketed and the $100-$250-$350 schedule quoted from the DSNY page was not confirmed. Opened NYC311: a business must hire a private carter or register as a self-hauler with the Business Integrity Commission, and must post the carter's decal; businesses that throw away less than 20 gallons a week may share a carter.

violations.name: Recyclables thrown out with the trash
violations.law: NYC Admin Code §16-306; 16 RCNY §1-10
violations.note: Read through search limited to nyc.gov: DSNY's set-out rules page for businesses gives $100 for the first offense, $200 for the second, $400 for the third and later. Opened at NYC311: every business must recycle metal, glass, rigid plastic, cartons and paper, post recycling signs and label its containers. Every business must recycle; a food business separates metal, glass, plastic, cartons, foil and cardboard from trash. A cafe throws out a lot of cardboard (milk and cup cases) and milk jugs. Food scraps: only shops of 7,000 sq ft or more, or chains with two or more city locations totalling 8,000 sq ft, must separate them, so a single small cafe is exempt.

violations.name: Resale certificate used for things you do not resell
violations.criminal: Issuing a false or fraudulent resale certificate with intent to evade tax can be prosecuted as a felony, and the state can revoke the Certificate of Authority, which shuts the register.

violations.name: CBD or another unapproved additive in drinks
violations.law: NYC Health Code §71.05 (adulterated food), §81.07
violations.note: Press reports from 2019 (CBS New York, Fox Business, Hemp Industry Daily): the Health Department barred restaurants and cafes from adding CBD to food or drinks, first embargoing the product on the shelf and, from October 1, 2019, writing fines of $200 to $650 by quantity; an earlier embargo hit activated charcoal. I did not find a 2026 city page confirming the amounts, so the range is from the press. Health Code section numbers cited from memory.

violations.name: Menu says organic, single-origin or oat; the cup holds something cheaper
violations.law: NYC Admin Code §20-700, §20-703 (Consumer Protection Law, as amended by Local Law 98 of 2021); NY General Business Law §349
violations.note: DCWP: Local Law 98 of 2021 raised the top fine for unfair trade practices seven-fold, from $500 to $3,500 per violation; each false statement is its own violation, and a knowing violation is $3,500. The department's penalty schedule for §20-700 lists $525, $1,050 and $3,500 (search summary of the rule text; I could not read which column is the first offense). Serving dairy to a customer who paid for oat is also an allergy hazard. Game formula: $525 in the first month, $1,050 in the second, capped at $3,500.

violations.name: Recalled product kept on sale
violations.law: NYC Health Code §71.05 (adulterated or misbranded food), §81.07; 21 U.S.C. §331
violations.criminal: Knowingly selling adulterated food that injures someone can be prosecuted under the federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
violations.note: NYC Health's guidance on adulterated food: the inspector has the product discarded and writes a summons with points toward the letter grade; the department's workshop slide gives a penalty of up to $1,200, and repeated violations can close the shop. A recall-specific line of the penalty schedule was not found; the $600 start is my game formula. The reputation hit stands for the news story, not the fine.

violations.name: Grab-and-go food with no allergen label
violations.law: NY Agriculture and Markets Law §199-g (effective November 12, 2026), §39

violations.name: Bottling or roasting for other stores with no state license
violations.law: NY Agriculture and Markets Law Article 20-C, §39

violations.name: Manual workers not paid weekly
violations.law: NY Labor Law §191(1)(a); §198(1-a) as amended May 9, 2025
violations.note: First violation by an employer who paid at least twice a month: interest only (16% a year, about 0.3% of the late wages). Half of a $13,456 monthly payroll is paid a week late: about $20 a month. A repeat violation owes 100% of the late-paid wages as liquidated damages - the engine should switch to perMonth = half the monthly payroll on the second finding.

violations.name: No pay notice at hire, no pay stubs
violations.law: NY Labor Law §195(1), §195(3), §198(1-b), §198(1-d) (Wage Theft Prevention Act); 12 NYCRR §146-2.2, §146-2.3

violations.name: Call-in pay not paid
violations.law: 12 NYCRR §146-1.5; NY Labor Law §198(1-a)

violations.name: Meal period not given
violations.law: NY Labor Law §162, §218
violations.note: Search-seen (primary, NY DOL meal period guidelines LS 443): at least 30 minutes for a shift of more than six hours that spans 11 am to 2 pm. Where only one person is on duty the Department accepts eating on the job if the worker voluntarily consents, but an uninterrupted meal period must be given to any worker who asks. The statute sets no dollar amount of its own; the game uses Labor Law 218: up to $1,000 for a first violation, $2,000 for a second, $3,000 after that (from the user's research report). Arithmetic for the saving: one hour a day of break relief x 30 days x $21 = $630. Opened: NY DOL guidelines LS 443: the 30-minute rule and the one-employee shift exception with voluntary consent. The penalty ladder was not opened.

violations.name: Unlawful deductions from wages
violations.law: NY Labor Law §193, §198(1-a); 12 NYCRR §146-2.7

violations.name: Required uniform not paid for or maintained
Managers or back-of-house staff in the tip pool
violations.note: Search-seen (primary, dol.gov): an employer may not keep employees' tips or let managers or supervisors keep them; a manager may keep only tips for service he or she "directly and solely" provides (opinion letter FLSA2026-13, September 2026). The employer owes the tips kept plus an equal amount as liquidated damages, and a civil money penalty of up to $1,100 per violation in the statute (adjusted upward each year; the 2026 figure was not in the results). Search-seen (secondary): New York's wage order limits tip pools to workers whose principal duty is personal service to customers, so a dishwasher or baker cannot be put in a required pool even though federal law would allow it when no tip credit is taken. Arithmetic: one of five shares of $2,000 in card tips = $400 a month. In April 2026 the US Labor Department recovered $85,000 for 36 workers at a coffee bar near Austin over tip pool violations. Opened: Part 146, section 146-2.14(e): eligibility is by duties, not titles; eligible occupations include wait staff and counter personnel who serve food or beverages. NY DOL tips FAQ: card tips due by the next regular payday, less the pro-rated card charge. The federal page was not opened (the site refused).

violations.name: Tip credit taken without notice, records or enough tips
Hourly worker put on a salary to avoid overtime
Retaliation against a worker who complained
violations.law: NY Labor Law §215; NYC Administrative Code §20-918, §20-924
violations.note: Search-seen (primary, NY DOL FAQ): employers who retaliate "can be fined up to $20,000". From memory of Labor Law 215 (page not opened): a civil penalty of $1,000 to $10,000, up to $20,000 for a repeat within six years, plus lost pay, reinstatement and liquidated damages of up to $20,000. Game formula, my estimate: $5,000 (middle of the first-violation range) plus $3,400 for each month of lost pay (160 h x $21), capped at $30,000 ($10,000 + $20,000). Search-seen (primary, nyc.gov): under the city Protected Time Off Law retaliation costs full compensation plus $500, or $2,500 if the worker was fired. Threatening to call immigration authorities counts as retaliation. Opened: NYC Protected Time Off FAQ: retaliation costs full compensation plus damages of $500 or $2,500. The NY DOL pages opened state no dollar amount for Labor Law 215.

violations.name: Minor working without papers or outside legal hours
violations.law: NY Labor Law §§130-133, §§142-143, §141 as amended May 9, 2025; 29 CFR Part 570

violations.name: Unpaid "volunteers" doing staff work
violations.law: NY Labor Law §652, §198(1-a); 12 NYCRR §146-1.2; 29 U.S.C. §206; NY Workers' Compensation Law §52
violations.note: A for-profit business may not accept free labor: anyone it "suffers or permits to work" is an employee owed at least $17.00 an hour (rate seen in the existing pack at NY DOL). Arithmetic: 40 hours a month x $17.00 x 1.1158 (employer payroll taxes) = $759. Owed back with 100% liquidated damages. The helper is also outside your workers' compensation policy until put on payroll, so an injury becomes an uninsured claim. Narrow exceptions exist for a sole proprietor's own spouse; I could not open a source that states them for a New York LLC, so do not rely on one.

violations.name: Cash tips kept off payroll
Firing or threatening workers for organizing
violations.law: 29 U.S.C. §157, §158(a)(1), §158(a)(3), §160(c) (National Labor Relations Act)
violations.note: Search-seen (secondary, https://www.buchalter.com/blogs/recreational-equipment-inc-and-united-food-commercial-workers-local-555-nlrb-alj-finds-unlawful-discharge-during-organizing-drive-but-denies-gissel-bargaining-order/): the labor board's remedies are make-whole, not fines: reinstatement, back pay with interest, and a posted or read notice (January 2026 judge's decision in a retail organizing case). Game formula: back pay for two organizers, 2 x 160 h x $21 = $6,720 a month, rounded to $6,800, running until they are rehired. The Act protects any two workers who act together about pay or conditions, union or not, and it covers a shop of five. Search-seen (secondary): a Brooklyn coffee shop's staff filed for a union unanimously in November 2022 after hours and pay were cut and won the first contract at an independent New York coffee shop. Opened: National Labor Relations Board pages 'Concerted Activity' (employees may act with co-workers about work issues: talk about wages, circulate a petition for better hours, go to the employer together) and 'Section 8(a)(3)' (an employer may not discharge, lay off or discipline employees because they support a union). The wording of the remedies was not on the pages opened.

violations.name: No day of rest in the week
violations.law: NY Labor Law §161, §218
violations.note: Search-seen (primary, NY DOL form LS 611 and Labor Law 161): an employer operating a restaurant must give every employee at least 24 consecutive hours of rest in each calendar week (Sunday to Saturday) and name the day in advance. The game uses the Labor Law 218 ladder: up to $1,000, $2,000, $3,000 (from the user's research report). A worker who agrees to a seventh day is not a defence without a Labor Department variance. Opened: NY DOL form LS 611: restaurants must give at least twenty-four consecutive hours of rest in any calendar week. The penalty ladder was not opened.

violations.name: No disability and Paid Family Leave insurance
violations.law: NY Workers' Compensation Law §211, §213, §220
violations.criminal: Failure to secure the coverage is a misdemeanor: a fine of $100 to $500 or up to one year in jail, or both (Workers' Compensation Board).

violations.name: No sexual harassment policy or yearly training
violations.law: NY Labor Law §201-g, §218; NYC Administrative Code §8-107(29)
violations.note: Labor Law §201-g: every employer, whatever its size, must adopt a written sexual harassment prevention policy at least as strong as the state model and give every employee interactive training every year. The section sets no fine of its own. Game formula uses Labor Law §218 for violations other than unpaid wages, as quoted in the research notes: up to $1,000 for a first violation, $2,000 for a second, $3,000 for a third. The larger cost is in court: with no policy and no training an employer loses its main defense in a harassment claim.

violations.name: Harassment complaint ignored
violations.law: NY Executive Law §296(1)(h), §297; NYC Administrative Code §8-107, §8-126
violations.note: Search-seen (secondary): since February 8, 2020 the New York State Human Rights Law covers every employer regardless of size, and harassment is anything above "petty slights or trivial inconveniences"; the federal law starts at 15 employees. Harassment by customers counts when the owner knew and did nothing. Search-seen (secondary, an insurer's figure): employment claims cost small businesses $27,000 to $54,000 a case on average; the game uses that band. The city Commission on Human Rights may add a civil penalty of up to $125,000, or $250,000 for a willful violation (search-seen, secondary). An employment practices policy pays the defence and the settlement above its deductible, not the lost staff.

violations.name: Job ad without a pay range
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §8-107(32); NY Labor Law §194-b
violations.note: NYC Human Rights Law: an employer with four or more workers must state the minimum and maximum pay in every job ad, a note in the window or an Instagram story included; the Commission can fine up to $250,000, but a first violation costs $0 if cured within 30 days. State Labor Law §194-b (in force since September 17, 2023): civil penalties up to $3,000. Game formula is my estimate: $1,000, capped at the state maximum. The city Commission also sends testers who answer ads.

violations.name: Asking about arrests, credit or past pay before an offer
violations.note: Search-seen (primary, NYC Commission on Human Rights Fair Chance FAQ): employers with four or more workers, the owner and contractors included, may not ask about criminal history until after a conditional job offer, and must give a written analysis and a chance to respond before taking the offer back. Search-seen (secondary): the same law bans credit checks for most jobs and questions about past pay; the Commission may impose up to $125,000, or $250,000 for a willful violation. The Commission also sends testers who pose as applicants. Game value $5,000 is my estimate of a small-employer settlement; I found no published average. Opened: NYC Commission on Human Rights Fair Chance FAQ: four or more employees including the owner and contractors; criminal records only after a conditional offer. Penalty amounts were not on the page.

violations.name: Fake or paid-for reviews
violations.law: 16 CFR Part 465 (FTC Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials); NY General Business Law §§ 349, 350; NYC Administrative Code § 20-700
violations.criminal: No; civil penalties. Fraud charges are possible only as part of a larger scheme.
violations.note: The FTC's question-and-answer page on the rule: in force since October 21, 2024; a business is liable for fake reviews it wrote or bought when it knew or should have known they were fake; reviews by officers or managers need a clear disclosure; paying for reviews is not banned as such, but a reward that depends on the review being positive is, stated or implied; civil penalties up to $53,088 per violation; consumers cannot sue under the rule. In December 2025 the FTC sent warning letters to ten companies. The $2,500 base is the smallest penalty in New York's 'Operation Clean Turf' (September 2013): the Attorney General ran a sting with a fake Brooklyn yogurt shop and settled with 19 companies for more than $350,000 in all (news reports). The reputation hit is my estimate of a public warning on the listing; the game's 'sting' route mirrors that operation.

violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-118(2)
violations.note: D11 correction between D07 (50/250/500) and D08 (100/50/300). Search-seen in the Sanitation penalty schedule as amended effective November 14, 2021: Administrative Code 16-118(2)(a) failure to clean the sidewalk and 18 inches into the gutter: $50 first offense, $100 second and third, $300 on default. perMonth 50 stands for the step from the first to the repeat offense. DSNY announced higher repeat-offender penalties from December 19, 2024; the new amounts were not found, so this may be low.

violations.law: 16 RCNY §1-02.1 (commercial containerization); NYC Administrative Code §16-120

violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §20-910(b) (Local Law 92 of 2015)

violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.07; 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 04C

violations.name: Refusing or obstructing a health inspection
violations.law: NYC Health Code §3.15(a); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 07A
violations.note: Appendix 23-C, code 07A: obstruction of Department personnel $1,000 (seen in the rule excerpt). The $2,000 ceiling is my assumption that the default penalty doubles, as it does for the grade card rows; the default figure was not in the excerpt. Locking the door, hiding the kitchen or keeping the inspector waiting all count, and the inspection then happens anyway.

violations.name: Candles or open flame without an FDNY permit
violations.law: NYC Fire Code FC 105.6, FC 308; 3 RCNY §109-03, Appendix A, Violation Category 3

violations.name: Required health signs and posters missing
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §17-172 (choking first aid poster), §17-188 (resuscitation equipment); NYC Health Code §81.21(c) (wash hands sign); NYC Health Code Article 81 (Healthy Eating Information poster)
violations.note: Seen at NYC Health: restaurants must post the choking first aid poster, the CPR equipment notice, the wash-hands sign, the no smoking sign and the Healthy Eating Information poster (alcohol and pregnancy warning if alcohol is served); the city gives all of them away free through 311. Seen: $200 for a missing Healthy Eating poster (NYC Health FAQ) and $200 for a missing wash-hands sign (2022 rule notice). The $200 per sign and the three-sign cap of $600 are my simplification; the penalty rows for the choking poster and the CPR kit were not in any excerpt I could read. Sign violations are unscored and many can be cured for $0 the first time (Local Law 80 of 2021). Section numbers 17-188 and 81.21(c) as cited by the sources.

violations.name: No food allergy notice on the menu, no allergen labels on packed food
violations.law: NY Public Health Law §1356 (allergy notice) and §1357 (allergen labels on food packed on the premises, in force since November 12, 2026); NYC Administrative Code §17-195

violations.name: Playing music without a public performance license
violations.law: 17 U.S.C. §§106(4), 501, 504(c); 17 U.S.C. §110(5)(B) (narrow exemption for radio and TV broadcasts in a food or drinking place under 3,750 sq ft)
