violations.note: Not a government fine: the licensing societies (ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, GMR) send letters, then a field agent notes the songs played, then they sue in federal court. Copyright law sets statutory damages of $750 to $30,000 per song and up to $150,000 if willful, plus the other side's legal fees. Seen in press: four Connecticut judgments against restaurants averaged just over $3,600 a song; a Massachusetts bar paid $15,000 for five songs; a Connecticut restaurant $18,000 for nine. Game formula is my estimate: four songs at the $750 minimum ($3,000) plus $500 for each month the letters were ignored, capped at $30,000. A personal Spotify or Apple Music account is not licensed for a business; the radio exemption does not cover streaming.

violations.name: Smoking or vaping allowed; no signs, no written policy
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §17-503, §17-508 (Smoke-Free Air Act)
violations.note: NYC Health: smoking and e-cigarette use are banned in restaurants, outdoor dining areas included; the owner must post no smoking and no vaping signs and keep a written smoking policy for staff. Penalties as described in the text of the 2002 act: $200 to $400 for a first violation, $500 to $1,000 for a second within 12 months, $1,000 to $2,000 for a third. I did not see the current penalty row, so the amounts are marked as an estimate. Section numbers cited from memory.

violations.name: Workers' rights poster not posted or handed out
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §32-102 (Local Law 161 of 2023)
violations.note: Law-firm alerts on Local Law 161 of 2023: since July 1, 2024 every NYC employer must post the city's 'Your Rights at Work' poster where staff can see it and give a copy to each worker, new hires on their first day; a first violation gets 30 days to cure, after that the civil penalty is $500. The statute itself was not opened, so this is marked as an estimate.

violations.name: Withheld payroll taxes not deposited
violations.criminal: Willfully failing to collect or pay over withheld tax is a federal felony: up to 5 years in prison and a $10,000 fine (26 U.S.C. §7202).

violations.name: Surcharge added on top of menu prices
violations.law: Rules of the City of New York, title 6, §5-59; NYC Administrative Code §20-700
violations.note: NYC DCWP inspection checklist: a restaurant may not add a surcharge to listed food and drink prices (its examples: a 5% living wage fee, a 20% administrative charge); a bona fide service charge is allowed only if conspicuously disclosed before food is ordered (a minimum per person, a plate-splitting charge, a mandatory tip for parties of eight or more). The fine was not on the pages opened; $350-$500 is the range of the city's consumer protection penalties as I know them, so the amounts are an estimate. A fee that reads like a tip also belongs to the staff under Labor Law §196-d.

violations.name: Taxable sales rung up as exempt
violations.criminal: Done on purpose it is the same crime as hiding sales: more than $3,000 of tax evaded within a year is a class E felony (Tax Law §1803).

violations.name: Payroll concealed from the workers' compensation insurer
violations.law: NY Workers' Compensation Law §52(1)(d), §52(5)
violations.note: NYS Workers' Compensation Board, 2026 conference material: an employer that intentionally and materially understates or conceals payroll, or misrepresents information used to calculate the premium, is deemed to have failed to secure compensation; the civil penalty is up to $2,000 for each 10-day period or up to twice the cost of compensation for the payroll in that period. Game formula follows the existing no_wc_insurance row: $6,000 a month plus twice the premium avoided. The insurer's own premium audit bills the missing premium first.

violations.name: Selling before the sales tax Certificate of Authority
violations.note: Amounts are those quoted in the existing _common roadmap step (from the DTF-17 instructions): up to $500 for the first day of business without a certificate and up to $200 for each day after, at most $10,000. The penalty bulletin opened this session lists only the $50 penalty for not displaying the certificate, so the row is an estimate. $200 x 30 days = $6,000 a month, capped at $10,000.

violations.name: Operating without hot and cold running water
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.20; 24 RCNY Chapter 23 (public health hazard)
violations.note: The penalty schedule lists inadequate potable water as a public health hazard; the dollar amount for running without hot and cold water was NOT found, $400 is a placeholder at the level of the pack's other health fines. An uncorrected public health hazard closes the shop.

officials.name: Health inspector
officials.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
officials.realProcess: Unannounced, at least once a year. The inspector walks the whole shop with a thermometer and a flashlight and scores each violation in points: under 14 is an A, and an A on the first visit also means no fines for the scored violations. With 14 or more, a second inspection comes about a month later and sets the grade; with 28 or more, inspectors keep coming about once a month. A hazard that cannot be fixed on the spot closes the shop. Fines are decided afterwards at the city tribunal (OATH).

officials.name: Outdoor dining inspector
officials.agency: NYC Department of Transportation (Dining Out NYC)
officials.realProcess: Inspectors patrol and answer 311 complaints. A licensed cafe with a setup problem first gets a corrective action request and 30 days to correct it; an unlicensed one is fined at once ($500, then $1,000) and can be ordered to clear the sidewalk.
officials.note: Same id as in the pack: one D02 violation added to the checks.

officials.name: Environmental inspector
officials.realProcess: Three separate units: sewer inspectors open the grease interceptor and ask for cleaning records; the cross-connection unit mails a notice when the yearly backflow test report is missing; noise inspectors answer 311 complaints and take a decibel reading inside the neighbor's home.

officials.name: Buildings inspector
officials.realProcess: Almost always sent by a 311 complaint: a neighbor hears demolition or sees a dumpster and no permit in the window. The inspector posts a Stop Work Order and writes a summons to OATH. The work must be legalized with filed plans before the order is lifted.

officials.name: Fire inspector
officials.realProcess: Fire inspectors and local firehouse companies walk through businesses unannounced and answer 311 complaints. They check extinguisher tags, exit paths, extension cords and permits, then write a violation order to fix it or a summons to the city tribunal (OATH), where the fine is halved if you prove the fix before the hearing.

officials.name: Sanitation enforcement agent
officials.realProcess: Sanitation enforcement agents walk commercial blocks in two fixed one-hour periods a day that depend on the address, and after every snowfall. They write a summons on the spot; no warning is required. The summons is answered at the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings or paid; an unanswered one defaults to the maximum penalty.

officials.name: Human rights investigator
officials.realProcess: The Commission takes complaints from the public and runs its own tests: testers answer job ads and visit businesses. Small employers are usually offered an early resolution: fix it, train the staff and pay a set penalty. A contested case goes to the city tribunal (OATH).

officials.name: State food inspector
officials.agency: NYS Department of Agriculture and Markets
officials.realProcess: The state licenses food processing and inspects food sold in packages. A complaint from a customer with an allergy, or from the shop that bought your bottles, brings an inspector who reads labels and asks for the license. Penalties are set under Agriculture and Markets Law §39 and can be settled with the department before they reach the attorney general.

officials.name: Federal wage and hour investigator
officials.agency: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
officials.realProcess: Investigators visit unannounced or after a complaint, interview staff in private and review two to three years of payroll and tip records. They recover tips and back wages for every affected worker and can add a civil money penalty for repeated or willful violations.

officials.name: Tip compliance examiner
officials.realProcess: The IRS compares card tips on merchant statements and the tips workers declare on their own returns with the tips on the employer's payroll filings, then sends a notice and demand for the employer share of the tax on the difference.

officials.name: Labor board agent
officials.agency: National Labor Relations Board, Region 2 (Manhattan) and Region 29 (Brooklyn)
officials.realProcess: A fired worker files a charge within six months. A board agent takes sworn statements; if the charge has merit the region seeks a settlement with reinstatement and back pay, or issues a complaint and tries the case before an administrative law judge.

officials.name: Disability and Paid Family Leave compliance officer
officials.realProcess: The Board matches employer records against active disability and Paid Family Leave policies and writes to employers with none on file. A worker whose claim is refused for lack of coverage triggers the same check, and the employer is billed for the claim.

officials.name: Civil court (private lawsuits)
officials.agency: U.S. District Court (S.D.N.Y. and E.D.N.Y.) and New York State Supreme Court
officials.realProcess: Not an inspector: a private party's lawyer files a complaint and a process server hands you the summons. Small businesses almost always settle within months, because the law makes the loser pay the other side's legal fees and a defense costs more than the settlement.

officials.name: IRS revenue officer
officials.realProcess: The IRS matches each quarterly Form 941 against the deposits it received. A revenue officer visits, interviews the owner (Form 4180) to decide who was responsible, and proposes the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty against that person. Liens and levies follow if nothing is paid.

reports.name: Report unsanitary conditions (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint about a food establishment. The Health Department sends an inspector unannounced; pests, dirty equipment, spoiled or home-made food all count. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report operating without a permit (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to the Health Department. An inspector checks the permit on the wall and asks who on the shift holds a Food Protection Certificate. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report unlicensed sidewalk tables or grease dumping (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint routed to the Transportation Department (outdoor dining) or Environmental Protection (grease in the sewer). An inspector checks the license and the grease interceptor. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report wage or tip theft (NYS Department of Labor)
reports.text: In real life: a labor standards complaint, which a worker or anyone else can file. An investigator audits time records, pay stubs and the tip log. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report construction or a sign without a permit (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to the Department of Buildings. An inspector looks for the permit in the window and can post a Stop Work Order the same day. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a cafe with no customer restroom (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to the Health Department. An inspector counts the seats; with 20 or more there must be a supplied toilet for customers. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report an overcrowded room or blocked exit (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint sent to the Buildings and Fire Departments. Inspectors compare the crowd with the Certificate of Occupancy, walk the exits and look into the cellar. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a sign without a permit (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to the Buildings Department, which may be anonymous. In 2018 such calls tripled and left hundreds of shops with $6,000 fines. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a blocked sidewalk or outdoor tables over the line (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint about signs, benches, goods or cafe tables in the walking path. Sanitation enforcement tickets obstructions; the Transportation Department measures outdoor cafes against their plans. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a barrier for disabled customers or an illegal job ad (Human Rights Commission)
reports.text: In real life: a complaint to the NYC Commission on Human Rights, which can also send testers. It checks the entrance, the service and the wording of help-wanted ads. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report loud music (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 noise complaint. An inspector from Environmental Protection takes a decibel reading inside the neighbor's home; over 42 decibels is a violation. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report no hot water or warm fridges (311)
reports.text: The Health Department sends an inspector to check the hand sinks and the fridge thermometers. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a fire hazard (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint routed to the Fire Department. Fire inspectors check extinguisher tags, exits, crowding and open-flame permits. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a noisy air conditioner or exhaust fan (311)
reports.text: The Department of Environmental Protection measures the noise from inside your home or your building. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report trash, recycling or banned packaging (311)
reports.text: The Sanitation Department sends an agent to look at the curb, the bins and the cups on the counter. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report fake reviews or false menu claims
reports.text: In real life: a complaint to the city's consumer protection department or the state Attorney General. Investigators check who wrote the reviews and whether the menu says what is in the cup. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report packaged food with no allergen label, or bottles sold without a state license
reports.text: The state food inspector reads the labels in the fridge and asks for the processing license. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report pay practices (NYS Department of Labor)
reports.text: In real life: a labor standards complaint, which any worker or member of the public can file. An investigator asks for schedules, time records, pay stubs and pay notices for the whole staff, going back up to six years. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report managers taking tips (US Department of Labor)
reports.text: In real life: a confidential complaint to the Wage and Hour Division, by phone or online. Investigators interview the staff and check who really shares the tips and what was reported to the IRS. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a minor working late or without papers
reports.text: In real life: a child labor complaint to the NYS Department of Labor. An investigator checks working papers and the schedule of every worker under 18. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report retaliation or missing workplace notices (NYS Department of Labor)
reports.text: In real life: a labor standards complaint, often filed by a former worker. An investigator asks who complained, what happened to their shifts, and for the harassment policy, training records and required posters. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report an illegal job ad or hiring question (NYC Commission on Human Rights)
reports.text: In real life: an online complaint or tip to the Commission. It checks the ad for a pay range and the application for questions about arrests, credit or past pay, and may send a tester. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report missing disability and family leave insurance
reports.text: In real life: a non-compliance report to the Workers' Compensation Board. The Board looks up the policy on file and writes to the employer. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a missing grade card, a pet inside or bare-hand food handling (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint about a food establishment. A health inspector checks the grade card in the window, the required signs, the hand sinks and how food is handled. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a hidden card fee or refused cash (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 consumer complaint to the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection. An inspector compares the posted prices with the receipt and tries to pay in cash. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report flyers on poles and cars (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to the Sanitation Department with a photo. Each flyer on public property is a separate fine for the business it advertises. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a dirty sidewalk or trash set out wrong (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to the Sanitation Department. An agent checks the sidewalk and gutter, the bins and lids, the carter's decal, foam cups and anything blocking the sidewalk. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a store cooling the street (311)
reports.text: Consumer and Worker Protection checks whether the door is propped open with the air conditioning on.

reports.name: Report getting sick after eating there (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 foodborne illness complaint. The Health Department interviews the person who got sick and sends an inspector to check temperatures, hand washing and where the food came from. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a missing backflow test or grease in the sewer (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to Environmental Protection. The department checks its records for the yearly backflow test report and sends an inspector to open the grease interceptor. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Tip off a music licensing society
reports.text: In real life: ASCAP, BMI and SESAC take tips and send field agents who sit in the shop and write down the songs. No license means letters, then a federal lawsuit. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report payroll taxes or insurance not being paid
reports.text: In real life: IRS Form 3949-A, or a fraud referral to the Workers' Compensation Board. Deposits are matched against payroll returns and the insurer audits the payroll. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

events.name: Wholesale coffee up 20%
events.text: Roasters pass on higher green coffee prices. Beans are about a quarter of what an order costs you to make.
events.note: Seen at FRED on November 14, 2026. Retail ground coffee (BLS APU0000717311, US city average): $9.457 per lb in June 2026, $9.249 in October 2026, a peak of $9.723 in April 2026. Green arabica (IMF PCOFFOTMUSDM, "Other Mild Arabica", cents per lb): 307.8 in June 2026, 359.2 in July 2026 (+16.7% in one month), 330.1 in September 2026; 276.8 in October 2024 and 409.5 in February 2025 (+48% in four months). Real signal for the event: the monthly arabica price up 15% or more. A 20% rise in the roaster's bean price x beans about 25% of cost of goods = +5% on cost of goods; both shares are my estimates.

events.name: Milk up 10%
events.text: Your dairy distributor raises prices. Milk goes into most of the drinks you sell.
events.note: Seen at FRED on November 14, 2026 (BLS APU0000709112, whole milk, US city average): $3.997 per gallon in November 2025, $4.317 in June 2026 (+8% in seven months), $4.101 in October 2026. The 10% rise and the dairy share of cost of goods (about 30%) are my estimates: 10% x 30% = +3%.

events.name: NYC Restaurant Week
events.text: Prix-fixe menus at $30, $45 and $60 pull diners into the neighborhood. More people walk past your door.
events.note: NYC Tourism, seen November 14, 2026: Restaurant Week Winter 2027 runs January 19 to February 11 with prix-fixe menus at $30, $45 and $60; Saturdays are excluded and restaurants may join for one to four weeks. A coffee shop does not sell prix-fixe meals: the 5% lift is my estimate for more people out on the streets of a dining block. No measurement exists.

events.name: Sidewalk shed goes up on your block
events.text: Scaffolding covers your storefront while the building repairs its facade. Fewer people notice the shop, and nobody can tell you when it comes down.
events.note: Fix of the existing event (was 0.9 for 3 months, both my predecessor's estimates). The city's 2024 study with Mastercard: restaurants and bars under a shed saw weekly transactions fall 3.5-9.7% in the six months after it went up; Manhattan businesses lost $3,900-$9,500 a month. 0.93 is the midpoint (6.6%). Length: the average shed permit in March 2026 was 557 days old (West Side Rag analysis of Buildings Department data), so 12 months is still short; the engine caps an event at a season.

events.name: Summer electricity peak
events.text: Air conditioning, ice machine and fridges run flat out while electricity is at its yearly high.
events.note: Research notes, NYSERDA statewide commercial average price: 22.3 cents per kWh in January 2026, 24.2 cents in July 2026: 8.5% higher. The page refused my request, so the figures are from the notes.

events.name: Flu season
events.text: Half the team is sick in the same fortnight. Sick workers are entitled to paid leave, and the bar runs short-handed.
events.note: Seen at DCWP: employers with 99 or fewer workers owe up to 40 hours of paid protected time off a year. The 8% loss of working hours is my estimate.

events.name: Buildings permits slow down
events.text: The Department of Buildings is taking longer to approve plans this season. Anyone still waiting for a permit waits a few days more.

events.name: Construction costs up 7%
events.text: Contractors in New York are quoting more than last year. A build-out not yet under contract costs more.
events.note: Page opened (Cushman & Wakefield Retail Fit-Out Cost Guide): national in-line retail fit-out $157 per sq ft in 2026, up 1.4%; "New York City ($181 psf)" among the most expensive markets. The 7.0% rise for New York was seen only in a search extract of the guide. That figure is plain retail, not food service. New field buildoutCost: applies to contracts signed while the event is active.

events.name: Tariff on European espresso machines
events.text: Italian machines and grinders carry a 15% import tariff. Dealers pass it on to new orders.
events.note: Trade press, seen in extract: since late July 2025 the United States applies a 15% tariff to goods from the European Union, appliances included. Full pass-through to the price of imported espresso machines and grinders is my assumption (upper bound); some dealers absorbed part of it. New field equipmentCost: applies to imported setup items bought while active.

events.name: One storefront in nine is empty
events.text: Landlords with empty stores are giving more free rent to sign a tenant. Leases signed now start cheaper.
events.note: Page opened (NYC Comptroller, "Who's Minding the Storefronts?"): the citywide storefront vacancy rate "remains elevated at 11.0% as of April 15, 2026. Currently, approximately 15,700 storefronts remain vacant"; Financial District-Battery Park City 21.1%, Ocean Hill 19.5%; Manhattan peaked at 15.8% in late 2023. Borough figures (Manhattan 12.9%, Brooklyn 12.3%, Queens 9.5%) are from the press release extract. The effect is a design value: one extra free month on a three-month concession (x1.33) in districts above the city average. New field freeRentMonths.

events.name: Someone reports every sign on the avenue
events.text: Dozens of sign complaints: Buildings inspectors walk the block.
events.note: Accessory storefront signs up to 150 sq ft carry no penalty under Local Law 15 of 2026.

events.name: Water and sewer rates go up on July 1
events.text: The Water Board raises rates every July. Ice, espresso, dishwashing and the restroom all run through the meter.
events.note: Water Board rate schedule effective July 1, 2026, read: metered water $5.35 per 100 cubic feet (it was $5.05 the year before: +5.9%), wastewater 159% of the water charge, so $13.86 combined; minimum charge $0.49 a day. Water is roughly a seventh of the pack's utilities line by my estimate (about 12 hundred-cubic-feet a month = $166 of $1,100): 5.9% x 15% = about 1%. The rates are verified; the cafe's water use is the estimate.

events.name: Card payments down for a day
events.text: Your payment company has an outage. Registers freeze or run offline, and shops across the city go cash-only for the day.
events.note: Real case: Square was down for most of a day on September 7-8, 2023; shops went cash-only. Game effect: one day of 30, with half of card customers walking away (90% pay by card): 1/30 x 0.9 x 0.5 = 1.5% of the month. The walk-away share is my estimate.

events.name: Water main break on your block
events.text: A main bursts under the street. The water is off until the city repairs it, and no water means no coffee and no hand washing.
events.note: Seen in the Mayor's Management Report: 552 water main breaks in fiscal 2025, the most since fiscal 2015 (7.9 per 100 miles of main). Game effect: one day closed out of 30 = 3.3%. The one-day duration is my estimate.

events.name: Planned water shut-off for street work
events.text: The city posts a notice: water off from morning until the end of the workday. You have 24 hours to fill containers or plan a short day.
events.note: Seen at the Department of Design and Construction: notices are posted at least 24 hours ahead, water goes off in the morning and is back by the end of the workday. Game effect: half a day of 30 = 1.5%.

events.name: Power failure in your Con Edison network
events.text: A feeder fails and the block goes dark for the afternoon. The register runs on battery; the fridges do not.
events.note: Seen in Con Edison's 2025 annual reliability report: in the underground network system 16.6 interruptions per 1,000 customers a year, lasting 6.70 hours on average; in the overhead system 439 per 1,000 and 2.02 hours. Game effect: half a day of sales = 1.5% of the month; spoiled stock is extra (see extra.mechanics).

events.name: Internet down across the neighborhood
events.text: A cut cable takes the internet out for most of a day. Shops without a backup line or offline mode cannot take cards.
events.note: Real cases: vandals cut a Spectrum fiber line in Queens in 2017, 60,000 customers were out for more than 15 hours and card sales stopped; Verizon Fios was down about 4 hours on November 12, 2024. Game effect for a shop with offline mode: 1% of the month.

events.name: Heat wave: fridges and ice machines fall behind
events.text: A week above 90°F. Compressors run without rest, ice machines cannot keep up, Con Edison lowers the voltage, and every technician in the city is booked.
events.note: Real cases: Con Edison cut voltage by 8% in parts of Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx in August 2022 (about 252,000 customers) and reduced voltage in Brooklyn and Staten Island in June 2025. Service calls for refrigeration and ice machines peak every June, July and August. The 3% loss of serving capacity is my estimate; staffAvailability is used because the engine has no equipment capacity target yet.

events.name: Finals and summer break
events.text: College terms end. Student baristas cut their hours for exams, then leave the city for the summer.
events.note: Seasonal pattern known to every shop near a campus; the 7% loss of hours is my estimate (one part-timer in a team of five working half hours for a month, then leaving). Announced for May. Search-seen (primary, bls.gov): the quits rate in accommodation and food services ran 3.6% to 5.0% a month in mid-2026.

events.name: Holiday week: everyone wants the same days off
events.text: Thanksgiving through New Year. Half the team asks for the same days and flies home.
events.note: The 10% loss of hours is my estimate. No law makes a private employer pay extra on holidays in New York, but the 32 unpaid protected hours a year (since February 22, 2026) can be used with no notice for the reasons the law covers, and many shops lose more to simple resignations after the holidays.

events.name: Summer hiring squeeze
events.text: Every patio, rooftop and ice cream window in the city is hiring at once. Good baristas have offers.
events.note: Search-seen (secondary): the National Restaurant Association projected about 450,000 seasonal restaurant jobs for summer 2026 and described soft hiring with low labor supply. The 2% wage pressure is my estimate (about 40 cents on a $21 wage).

events.name: A chain on your block raises barista pay
events.text: The chain two doors down posts a new starting wage. Your staff read the same job boards.
events.note: Search-seen (secondary, 2026 job postings): a venture-backed coffee chain lists New York baristas at $17 to $18 an hour plus tips and shift leads at $21; the largest chain's flagship lists $18.39 to start and $19.31 after certification. The 3% is my estimate of the raise an independent gives to keep people when a neighbour moves up by about $1.

events.name: City enforcement push on protected time off
events.text: The city worker-protection agency announces a data-driven sweep of employers with sick leave complaints.
events.note: Search-seen (primary, nyc.gov, February 2026): the mayor announced the expansion of protected time off for 4.3 million workers together with a new data-driven enforcement strategy. The 1.5x inspection rate is a game-balance value. Opened: the mayor's February 2026 release (4.3 million workers, new enforcement strategy, 32 unpaid hours on hire).

events.name: Federal I-9 audit notices reach restaurants
events.text: Immigration and Customs Enforcement serves notices of inspection. Employers get three business days to hand over every Form I-9.
events.note: Search-seen (secondary, law firms, April and October 2026): on March 16, 2026 ICE reclassified many common Form I-9 errors as substantive violations subject to immediate penalties; paperwork fines run $288 to $2,861 per form. The three business days are the standard notice period (from memory). The 1.3x is a game-balance value.

events.name: Work permits end for a group of workers
events.text: A federal protected-status program ends. Workers who relied on it lose permission to work on the stated date and must show other documents or stop.
events.note: Search-seen (secondary, law firms, June and July 2026): after a Supreme Court ruling, Temporary Protected Status ended for several countries in July and August 2026; employers had to re-verify affected workers on Form I-9 Supplement B on the effective date, not before. The National Restaurant Association and the New York State Restaurant Association asked for a 90 to 120 day transition. Search-seen (secondary): an industry study counted about 4,800 restaurant workers gone from New York City since March 2025. The 6% is my estimate.

events.name: Stomach bug goes through the team
events.text: One sick barista becomes three. Food workers with vomiting or diarrhea may not work, and they are entitled to protected time off.
events.note: The 15% loss of hours is my estimate: three of five people out for four days each. Sick food workers must be kept away from food under the city Health Code (see the health researcher's part for the code and the fine). Search-seen (primary, nyc.gov Protected Time Off FAQ): no documentation may be required for an absence of three or fewer consecutive work days.

events.name: A barista is called for jury duty
events.text: A summons arrives. Jury service in New York City can take a few days or two weeks, and the job is protected.
events.note: Search-seen (secondary; also nycourts.gov juror pay guidance): since June 8, 2025 the juror fee is $72 a day; employers with more than 10 employees pay the first three days (the lower of $72 and the daily wage), smaller employers need not pay. The 5% is my estimate: one of five people out for a quarter of the month.

events.name: A coffee chain opens on your block
events.text: A national chain takes the corner unit 150 meters away. Commuters who only want a fast cup now have a second door to choose from.
events.note: No controlled measurement exists for an independent cafe. Owners' accounts: one saw 10% of afternoon sales go when a Starbucks opened and won it back with breakfast sandwiches; a Hanover, New Hampshire cafe reported falling sales; in Minneapolis one neighbor lost coffee sales and another none. Between identical stores the measured effect is small: 1.2% per extra Starbucks within a mile (Marketing Science, 2018). 7% for six months is my planning value inside a 0-15% range.

events.name: The chain store down the block closes
events.text: The chain did not renew its lease. Its regulars need a new morning stop this week, and habits formed now tend to stay.
events.note: Center for an Urban Future, 2025 chain census: Starbucks closed 42 New York City stores in a year, more than any chain that stayed; chains as a whole fell 1.3% (112 stores), the sixth decline in eight years. The 6% gain for the nearest independent is my estimate.

events.name: A coffee cart sets up by the subway stairs
events.text: A licensed cart now sells drip coffee and a roll for about half your price, right where commuters come up from the train.
events.note: Intro 431, enacted over a veto in January 2026: 2,200 more mobile food vendor supervisory license applications each year from 2026 through 2031, on top of 6,880 existing food vendor permits. Carts work the warm months. 4% is my estimate: the cart takes drip coffee from commuters, not lattes from regulars.

events.name: January slump
events.text: New Year's resolutions, cold mornings and empty offices. Cafe owners say customers disappear at the start of every year.
events.note: Fresh Cup: coffee shop customers 'notoriously disappear at the beginning of every year'. Placer.ai: office visits stay low from Thanksgiving through the first weeks of January; the first and fourth quarters underperform. The 8% is extra.monthCurve's January value against an average month, my estimate.

events.name: Autumn drink season
events.text: The chains launch their autumn drinks in late August and customers go looking for something seasonal. Shops with a drink of their own share in it.
events.note: Placer.ai: Starbucks visits rose 3.4% in October and 14.7% in November 2021 month over month, its usual seasonal climb; visits ran 44.5% above average on the holiday drink launch day in November 2025. 3% for a neighborhood shop is my estimate, and it should apply only to shops that run the limited_time_drink lever.

events.name: Offices empty out for the holidays
events.text: From Thanksgiving week to the first days of January the office towers thin out. Morning lines shorten everywhere that lives on commuters.
events.note: Placer.ai: office visits in December 2025 were 33.1% under 2019, against 21.8% under in July 2025, and that was the busiest December since the pandemic. The 7% is for a mixed neighborhood block; an office-district shop loses far more (extra.eventCatalog holiday_office_exodus).

events.name: Summer Fridays
events.text: From late July to Labor Day the offices run half empty, most of all on Fridays. Residents are away too.
events.note: Placer.ai's August 2025 index: 'an end of summer slump'; Kastle card swipes dip in the week of July 4 and from late July to Labor Day. New York's Friday share of office visits was 11.9% in the first half of 2026. 4% for a mixed block is my estimate.

events.name: Peak visitor season
events.text: Hotels are full and the sidewalks are slow. Visitors find cafes on a map: the rating and the photos do the selling.
events.note: CoStar: New York City hotel occupancy led the 25 largest US markets at 87.9% in May 2025, 86.6% in September and 89.4% in October. New York had 65 million visitors in 2025 and forecasts 66.3 million for 2026. 5% for an average block is my estimate; tourist corridors gain more.

events.name: Delivery keeps growing
events.text: New Yorkers place more app orders every year, even with higher courier pay. A cafe that is not listed does not see those orders.
events.note: City report of October 21, 2026: 3.3 million app orders a week by June 2026, 700,000 more than in December 2023; consumer demand up 29% since 2023; the courier minimum is $22.13 an hour since April 1, 2026. 29% over about two and a half years is close to 10% a year; 8% is used.

events.name: Customers trade down
events.text: Households cut small luxuries first. Quick-service visits are falling across the country and a $7 latte is easy to skip.
events.note: Placer.ai: quick-service restaurant visits were 1.3% lower in the first seven months of 2026 than a year earlier, and 4.5% lower in May. Starbucks' US transactions fell 10% in its fourth fiscal quarter of 2024. 4% for an independent is my estimate between the two.

events.name: Campus summer break
events.text: Classes end in May and the students leave until September. The afternoon tables are suddenly free.
events.note: NYU's 2026-27 calendar: fall classes start September 2, 2026 and end December 14, exams December 16-22; spring classes start January 19, 2027. CUNY had about 247,000 students in fall 2025. 5% is my estimate for a mixed East Village block; a shop on the campus edge loses about 12% (the place model on the keen-cray branch).

events.name: World Cup summer
events.text: World Cup matches across the river and fans from everywhere in town. Shops that give them a reason to stop do well; a shop next to a closed street does not.
events.note: June 11 - July 19, 2026. Restaurant transactions in New York and New Jersey ran 18.5% higher during the group stage (trade roundup); venues that showed the matches reported 63% higher sales (NYC Hospitality Alliance survey); hotel room revenue rose 20.6%; one restaurant a five-minute walk from the stadium reported 60% lower sales on match days. 4% for an ordinary cafe is my estimate.

events.name: Wildfire smoke
events.text: Smoke from Canadian wildfires pushes the Air Quality Index over 150 for three days. People stay inside.
events.note: Short form of the catalog event: three days at 0.8 = 2% of a month. Index 289 on July 16-19, 2026; 465-484 in June 2023.

events.name: No weekend trains at your station
events.text: Signal work shuts your subway line on weekends. Shops near the stations lose a fifth of their weekend sales.
events.note: Short form of the catalog event. Greenpoint survey 2025-26: sales down 20-24% on shutdown weekends.

events.name: Water main replacement on your block
events.text: The street is fenced and trenched for a year. The city pays nothing for the sales you lose.
events.note: Short form of the catalog event. One West 10th Street shop: receipts down 10-15%.

events.name: The clocks go back
events.text: Dark at five. Afternoon walk-ins thin out for two months.
events.note: Short form of the catalog event. JPMorgan Chase Institute: daily card spending -3.5% after the clocks go back.

events.name: Con Edison rates rise
events.text: A three-year Con Edison rate plan took effect on January 1, 2026: a typical commercial electric bill is up about 3% this year, with further steps in 2027 and 2028.

events.name: Blizzard
events.text: A foot of snow. The city asks people to stay home for two days, and you have four hours to clear your sidewalk when it stops.
events.note: Short form of the catalog event: two days at 0.4 = 4% of a month, rounded.

events.name: Insurance renewal: premiums up 7%
events.text: Insurers raise rates across the city. Your business policy renews at a higher price for the next twelve months.
events.note: Manhattan Chamber of Commerce figures reported by Bloomberg and Insurance Journal on October 14, 2026: over the last year business insurance for New York-area service firms rose 7%, employee health insurance 12.9%, utilities 8.5%, wages 3.4%. One bar owner's liability premium grew fivefold in four years to $24,000. Applied as the citywide average.

events.name: Workers' compensation rates fall
events.text: The state approves lower workers' compensation loss costs from October 1. Your premium drops at the next renewal.
events.note: NYS Department of Financial Services, July 15, 2026: a 21.9% decrease in the overall loss cost level from October 1, 2026, after 13.2% the year before. Each insurer multiplies the loss cost by its own filed factor, so an employer's premium falls by less: game value -15%.

events.name: Prime rate up a quarter point
events.text: Banks raise the prime rate. Variable-rate loans, credit lines and cards cost more from next month.
events.note: The Wall Street Journal prime rate was 6.75% in spring 2026 and has been 7.00% since September 16, 2026 (Bankrate and rate trackers, November 2026). A quarter point on a 13% SBA loan is 13.25 / 13 = x1.02: about $14 a month per $100,000 borrowed.

events.name: Card processor adds 5 cents per tap
events.text: Your processor changes its pricing. On small tickets the cents matter more than the percentage.
events.note: Square says its in-person rate moved to 2.6% + 15 cents on February 25, 2025; the earlier per-tap fee was 10 cents (from memory). On an $8.50 order that takes the fee from about 32 cents to 37 cents. The pack already uses 15 cents; the event is a template for the next change.

events.name: Minimum wage may rise to $17.60 on March 1
events.text: The wage floor stayed at $17.00 on January 1. The Governor has proposed $17.60 from March 1, 2027; it needs a vote in Albany.
events.note: NYS Governor's page: on January 1, 2027 the minimum wage stays at $17.00 in New York City because one of the law's off-ramp conditions was met; the Governor proposed inflation-based increases from March 1, 2027: $17.60 downstate, subject to legislation. 17.60 / 17.00 = 1.035. The pack pays $21, so the direct effect is on new hires and on the wage ladder; apply only if the bill passes.

events.name: Offices call people back
events.text: Weekday mornings fill up in office districts.
events.note: Kastle: peak-day occupancy 87.3% in New York City on October 27, 2026. Prime tier only.

events.name: Your rating drops a star
events.text: One star less on review sites costs an independent restaurant 5-9% of revenue.
events.note: Luca (Harvard Business School): one star = 5-9% of revenue for independents. Triggered by the player's own quality, not by chance.

events.name: Delivery apps push the enhanced plan
events.text: Apps offer top placement for up to 20% more commission. Restaurants that stay on the basic plan slide down the list.
events.note: Local Law 79 of 2025 (Intro 762-B) keeps the 23% cap for the basic plan and allows an optional enhanced tier up to 20% more. The 10% loss of delivery orders on the basic plan is my estimate.

events.name: Con Edison shuts off gas to the building
events.text: A leak test finds bad piping upstairs. Gas stays off until the landlord's plumber passes a new test.
events.note: News 12: Con Ed shut off gas to a Fordham building after finding illegal plumbing work; the restaurant was told 6-8 months. Hits gas kitchens and bakeries; electric-only cafes are spared. The 15% loss (cold menu only) is my estimate.

events.name: A snowy month
events.text: Several snowfalls are forecast. Every one starts a 4-hour clock to clear your sidewalk, and fewer people walk on slush.
events.note: Quoted in search excerpts: Fiserv, January 2026: limited-service restaurant sales -3.4% and traffic -5.0% year over year in a month of storms. The snow days themselves come from the weather series (footTrafficMult snow 0.85, storm 0.7 in ai/src/data/nyc-climate.json); this event is the month-wide drag. Monthly 0.95 = the Fiserv traffic figure.

events.name: Rent goes up 3%
events.text: Your lease anniversary: the rent steps up by the percentage written in the lease.

events.name: Store rents keep climbing
events.text: New leases on Manhattan corridors cost more each quarter.
events.note: CBRE Q3 2026: +5% a year; one quarter. Applies to leases signed while active.

events.name: Empty storefronts give tenants leverage
events.text: On a block with many empty stores, landlords cut rent for new tenants.
events.note: Cheap tier only; Manhattan availability at a record low 9.8% in Q3 2026.

events.name: Staying past the end of the lease
events.text: The lease ran out during talks. Every month is billed at the holdover rate.
events.note: D08 eventCatalog: The engine clamps multipliers at 1.5; leases reported in court decisions set 150%, 200%, or 150% rising to 200% after 30 days.

events.name: The renewal letter
events.text: Six months before the lease ends the landlord names the new rent at today's market.
events.note: Mid tier; prime 1.3, cheap 1.05 (eventCatalog).

events.name: A shed hides your sign
events.text: A sidewalk shed goes up and covers your sign.
events.note: D00 eventCatalog: Deterministic qualitative scenario derived from source; numerical impact is not calibrated. Empty months means any month with the stated signal. National surveys and foreign stories do not establish NYC cafe coefficients.

events.name: Buildings sweep for unpermitted work
events.text: Inspectors check every build-out on the block without waiting for a complaint.

events.name: The electric bill jumps
events.text: New equipment pushed your peak load into demand charges.
events.note: D02 eventCatalog: Third-party rate summaries put the demand delivery charge for Con Edison's general large class at about $34.50 per kW in winter and $44.05 in summer; the official tariff and the 10 kW threshold were not confirmed. The 10% is a game value.

ruleCards.title: Letter grades
ruleCards.text: Every NYC cafe is inspected unannounced at least once a year. 0-13 points is an A, 14-27 a B, 28 or more a C, and the card must hang where passersby can see it. Not posting it costs $500; tampering with it costs $1,000.

ruleCards.title: Food Service Establishment Permit
ruleCards.text: A cafe needs a Food Service Establishment Permit from the Health Department: $280 a year. You may open on the 22nd day after applying even if no inspector has come yet; the first inspection then arrives unannounced.

ruleCards.title: No permit
ruleCards.text: Serving food or drinks without a current Health Department permit costs $1,000 ($2,000 if you ignore the summons), and the Department can order the shop closed until the permit is issued.

ruleCards.title: Food Protection Certificate
ruleCards.text: A certified supervisor must cover food receiving and preparation as well as public opening hours. A certificate held by someone who is absent does not provide coverage. Arrange qualified relief before the opening shift.

ruleCards.title: Clean, rinse, sanitize
ruleCards.text: Surfaces that touch food must be washed, rinsed and sanitized. A dirty steam wand, grinder or cutting board is a critical violation: $200-$300 and 5 to 8 points each time. Dirty floors and walls add $100 and 2 to 5 points.

ruleCards.title: Pests
ruleCards.text: Mice, rats or roaches cost $200-$350 per citation and 5 to 28 points: at the worst level that alone is a C. The Health Code also requires a contract with a licensed exterminator kept on site ($100 if it is missing).

ruleCards.title: Food safety depends on handling
ruleCards.text: Calendar age alone does not make food unsafe. Apply the food-specific source, storage, cooling, reheating and contamination rules. Stop selling food whose safe handling cannot be established.

ruleCards.title: Check the actual approved source
ruleCards.text: Use approved suppliers. A qualifying registered NY home processor may supply permitted packaged goods; that does not authorize a cafe operator to make its own menu at home. Check the supplier, product and labeling.

ruleCards.title: Tips belong to the staff
ruleCards.text: Tips belong to the workers. An owner or manager may not keep any part of them (NY Labor Law §196-d). Taken tips are owed back with 100% damages and interest, and claims reach back six years.

ruleCards.title: Trial shifts are paid
ruleCards.text: Trial shifts, training and staff meetings are work. Each hour must be paid at $17.00 or more, and anyone who reports for a shift is owed at least 3 hours of pay. Unpaid hours are owed back double.

ruleCards.title: Spread of hours
ruleCards.text: If a workday stretches over more than 10 hours from start to finish, breaks and split shifts included, the worker is owed one extra hour at the minimum wage: $17.00 in New York City.

ruleCards.title: Sidewalk tables
ruleCards.text: Tables on the sidewalk need a Dining Out NYC license: $1,050 for four years, a $1,500 deposit and a yearly fee of $6-$31 per square foot. Without it: $500 for the first offense, $1,000 for each one after, and the city can remove the setup.

ruleCards.title: Outdoor dining takes a long time
ruleCards.text: Plan the first year without outdoor seats. The city Comptroller found in 2026 that more than half of the restaurants approved for outdoor dining had waited over 19 months for the permit.

ruleCards.title: Grease interceptor
ruleCards.text: Coffee shops need a grease interceptor too: milk fat counts. It must be properly sized and installed, and cleaned before grease fills 25% of it. Fines run from $100 to $1,500.

ruleCards.title: The 20-seat line
ruleCards.text: With 20 or more seats, counting outdoor ones, a cafe must give customers a bathroom. Under 20 seats you do not need a customer bathroom, but you still need a hand-washing sink near the bar and in every restroom.

ruleCards.title: Tipped wage
ruleCards.text: A tipped food service worker in NYC may be paid $11.35 in cash plus a $5.65 tip credit only with written notice, records, and tips that really cover the gap. Otherwise the full $17.00 is due. The safe choice is to pay the full wage.

ruleCards.title: What is taxed in a cafe
ruleCards.text: Coffee in a cup is taxed at 8.875% even to go. Food eaten in the shop, heated food and sandwiches are taxed too. Bags of beans to take home are not. Set the register up item by item: the tax you collect is never part of your sales.

ruleCards.title: Card fees on small tickets
ruleCards.text: Card fees are not just 2.5%. With 15 cents per tap, and the fee charged on tax and tips too, an $8.50 order costs about 35 cents to process: around 4% of sales. Small tickets pay the highest share.

ruleCards.title: After a bad inspection
ruleCards.text: Score 14 or more on the first inspection and the inspector returns no sooner than 7 days later to set your grade. A B brings the next cycle in 5-7 months, a C in 3-5 months, instead of once a year.

ruleCards.title: Storefront signs
ruleCards.text: A wall sign of 6 square feet or less needs no Buildings Department sign permit. Anything bigger needs a permit that only a licensed sign hanger can obtain. Read the lease as well: the landlord usually has to approve the sign.

ruleCards.title: Business trash
ruleCards.text: The city does not collect business trash. You must sign with a private carter authorized for your commercial waste zone (three per zone) and post its decal. Each carter has a maximum price that depends on how much you put out.

ruleCards.title: Fair Workweek
ruleCards.text: New York City's Fair Workweek Law covers fast food chains with 30 or more locations nationwide: schedules 14 days ahead and premiums for changes. One independent cafe is not covered, but call-in pay and spread-of-hours rules still apply.

ruleCards.title: Check a former cafe before buying
ruleCards.text: An existing fit-out can save work, but confirm permitted use, equipment condition, lease consent and new permits. Follow bulk-sale procedures before paying for or taking possession of business assets.

ruleCards.title: Permits before the hammer
ruleCards.text: Moving plumbing, adding outlets or building walls needs a Buildings permit. Work without one costs 21 times the permit fee, at least $6,000 and up to $15,000, plus a Stop Work Order; working through the order is another $6,000.

ruleCards.title: Licensed plumber, licensed electrician
ruleCards.text: In New York City only a licensed master plumber may do plumbing and only a licensed electrician may wire. Unlicensed work is a misdemeanor with civil penalties from $2,500, cannot pass inspection, and gets torn out and redone.

ruleCards.title: Practice inspection from the city
ruleCards.text: The Health Department sells practice inspections: $100 for a new restaurant before its first graded visit, $400 after. No violations are written, but a public health hazard must still be fixed on the spot.

ruleCards.title: Bulk sale notice
ruleCards.text: A buyer of business assets must file Form AU-196.10 with the Tax Department at least 10 days before paying or taking possession. Miss it and you personally owe the seller's unpaid sales tax, up to the purchase price or the assets' value.

ruleCards.title: Key money
ruleCards.text: Key money buys a lease and whatever is bolted to the room, not a customer base. It is worth paying only when the inherited rent is below market and enough years remain. New York listings range from $30,000 for a small cafe to $225,000 for a Village storefront.

ruleCards.title: The space must be legal for a cafe
ruleCards.text: The building's Certificate of Occupancy has to allow your kind of business; a pre-1938 building needs a Letter of No Objection instead. Occupancy contrary to the certificate is fined $400 to $25,000, and only the owner can file to amend it.

ruleCards.title: Seat 20 needs a toilet
ruleCards.text: A cafe with 20 or more seats, outdoor ones included, must give customers a toilet they can reach without crossing the kitchen or storage. No toilet: $300 and 10 points at every inspection. Premises with a food permit by December 5, 1977 are exempt until they renovate.

ruleCards.title: A stocked restroom
ruleCards.text: A restroom without toilet paper, a waste bin or a self-closing door costs $200 and 2 to 5 points at inspection. A one-person restroom must also carry an all-gender sign on the wall next to the door (Local Law 79 of 2016).

ruleCards.title: Access lawsuits
ruleCards.text: Lawyers filed 8,667 federal disability-access suits in 2025; New York led in website suits with 1,021. A step at the door or a site a screen reader cannot use is enough. Half of what you spend on fixes returns as a tax credit, up to $5,000 a year.

ruleCards.title: The sign needs a permit too
ruleCards.text: A sign over 6 square feet needs a Buildings permit and a licensed installer. One 311 complaint can bring a work-without-a-permit fine of $6,000. In 2018-2019 whole avenues of shop signs were reported at once.

ruleCards.title: Your sign on their sidewalk
ruleCards.text: An A-frame sign may stand no more than 3 feet out from your wall and no taller than 5 feet. Beyond that, signs, benches and crates are sidewalk obstructions: $50 the first time, $100 each time after, $300 if you ignore the ticket.

ruleCards.title: Backflow test
ruleCards.text: The backflow valve on your water line must be tested every year by a certified tester and the report sent to the city. A missing report: $500, cut to $50 if you file it before the hearing, $1,000 if you ignore the ticket.

ruleCards.title: Air you have to maintain
ruleCards.text: The Health Code requires working ventilation. Ventilation that is missing, badly installed or broken costs $200 and 2 to 5 points at inspection. Most leases make the tenant, not the landlord, pay for the air conditioning unit.

ruleCards.title: Open door, air conditioning on
ruleCards.text: Since 2015 NYC shops must shut doors and windows while the air conditioning runs. A food business with indoor seating whose door opens straight to the street is exempt; with a vestibule between door and seats it is not. The city made nearly 6,300 inspections in 2024.

ruleCards.title: Outdoor tables over the line
ruleCards.text: A licensed outdoor cafe that breaks the design or operating rules first gets a corrective action request and 30 days to fix it. After that: $200 for the first offense, $500 for each later one, and repeat offenders can lose the license.

ruleCards.title: Candles need a permit
ruleCards.text: Candles on the tables need a Fire Department open flame permit in any restaurant, even one for fewer than 75 people: $210 a year. No lit candles where people stand, in an aisle or at an exit.

ruleCards.title: Fridges must hold 41°F
ruleCards.text: Cold food must stay at 41°F or below. A fridge that cannot hold it is a critical violation, $300-$350; the warm milk inside is a second one, $250-$600 and 7 to 28 points. Replace the fridge before the inspector does it for you.

ruleCards.title: Drains and air gaps
ruleCards.text: Ice machines, fridges and air conditioners must drain into a proper drain, not a bucket or the sidewalk, and water lines need backflow protection. Inspectors cite it under code 10B: 2 to 5 points each time.

ruleCards.title: A thermometer in every fridge
ruleCards.text: Each refrigerator needs an accurate thermometer in its warmest part (code 10E), and the shop needs a probe thermometer for food: without one the fine is $200-$300. A $10 thermometer is the cheapest insurance in the shop.

ruleCards.title: Noisy equipment
ruleCards.text: An air conditioner or exhaust fan may not be louder than 42 decibels inside a neighbor's home, measured three feet from an open window. A complaint brings an inspector with a meter: $220-$600, waived the first time if you prove you fixed it.

ruleCards.title: You must hire a carter
ruleCards.text: The city does not pick up business trash: hire a private carter or register as a self-hauler. In a live waste zone you choose among three carters; miss the deadline and one is assigned at the maximum rate. Caps: $26.87 per cubic yard or $17.64 per 100 lb.

ruleCards.title: The corner basket is not yours
ruleCards.text: City litter baskets are for pedestrians. Shop trash in one is illegal, and a cup with your name on it counts as proof. Every business must hire a licensed private carter or register to haul its own; under 20 gallons a week, you may share a carter.

ruleCards.title: Business recycling
ruleCards.text: Every business must recycle. A cafe separates metal, glass, plastic, cartons and cardboard from trash: $100, $200, then $400. Food scraps must be separated only by shops of 7,000 sq ft or chains; one small cafe is exempt.

ruleCards.title: Bins with lids
ruleCards.text: Since March 2024 business trash goes to the curb in bins with secure lids, one hour before closing or after 8 PM, and the bins come back in by opening time. $50, then $100, then $200 every time after.

ruleCards.title: What you can buy tax-free
ruleCards.text: Cups, lids, sleeves, bags and wrappers go home with the customer: buy them tax-free with a resale certificate. Napkins, straws, stirrers, utensils, cleaning supplies and equipment are taxed. Misuse costs 100% of the tax plus $50 a document.

ruleCards.title: The menu is a promise
ruleCards.text: Organic, single-origin, local, oat: every word on the menu must be true of what is in the cup. Each false claim is a separate deceptive practice; fines were raised in 2021 from $500 to as much as $3,500 per violation.

ruleCards.title: When a product is recalled
ruleCards.text: A recall names brands, sizes and lot codes. Check your shelves the same day, pull what matches, keep the supplier's credit note. Food under recall is adulterated food: a summons of up to $1,200 and points toward your grade.

ruleCards.title: Five cents a paper bag
ruleCards.text: Hand a customer a paper carryout bag for beans, bottles or packaged goods and you collect 5 cents, shown as its own line with the number of bags. A bag holding only food sliced or prepared to order is exempt. The fee goes in with your sales tax return.

ruleCards.title: State license to bottle or roast
ruleCards.text: Bottling coffee or roasting beans for sale beyond your own counter needs a state Article 20-C license. Without it: up to $600 for a first violation and up to $1,200 for each later one, and every day of production counts separately.

ruleCards.title: Weekly pay
ruleCards.text: Counter staff count as manual workers, and New York requires paying them every week (Labor Law §191). Since 2025 a first violation costs interest on the late wages; a repeat costs damages equal to all the wages paid late.

ruleCards.title: Pay notice and pay stubs
ruleCards.text: Give each hire a written pay notice in English and their main language, and a pay stub every payday. No notice: $50 per work day. No stubs: $250 per work day. Each is capped at $5,000 per worker. A new notice is due before any pay change.

ruleCards.title: Call-in pay
ruleCards.text: A worker who shows up for a shift is owed at least 3 hours of pay, or the scheduled shift if shorter, even if you send them home after 20 minutes because it is raining or the power is out (12 NYCRR 146-1.5).

ruleCards.title: Meal periods
ruleCards.text: A shift of more than 6 hours that covers 11 am to 2 pm includes a 30-minute meal period. On a one-person shift the worker may agree to eat on the job, but anyone who asks for an uninterrupted break must get one (NY Labor Law 162).

ruleCards.title: Deductions from pay
ruleCards.text: You may not take cash shortages, breakage, walkouts or fines out of a worker's pay, or make them pay you back in cash. Only deductions required by law or agreed in writing for the worker's own benefit are legal (NY Labor Law 193).

ruleCards.title: Uniforms
ruleCards.text: If you require a logo shirt or apron, you pay for it. Unless you supply enough wash-and-wear sets you also owe weekly uniform maintenance pay: $21.10 for over 30 hours, $16.75 for 20 to 30, $10.10 for 20 or fewer (NYC, 2026).

ruleCards.title: Who may share tips
ruleCards.text: Only workers who serve customers may share tips: baristas, counter staff, and shift leads with no real authority over others. Managers and owners may never take a share, and New York does not allow a required pool to include the dishwasher or baker.

ruleCards.title: Tip credit paperwork
ruleCards.text: The $11.35 tipped wage (a $5.65 tip credit) is legal only with written notice before the first shift, tip records, and tips that really cover the gap. Miss one and the full $17.00 was due for every hour, going back six years.

ruleCards.title: Salary does not end overtime
ruleCards.text: A title does not end overtime. In NYC in 2026 an exempt manager needs a salary of at least $1,275 a week ($66,300 a year) and must really manage. Everyone else is paid by the hour and gets 1.5 times the rate after 40 hours.

ruleCards.title: No retaliation
ruleCards.text: You may not fire, cut hours or threaten a worker for complaining about pay, sick leave or safety, even if the complaint is wrong. Under NY Labor Law 215 the state can fine up to $20,000, on top of lost pay and damages.

ruleCards.title: Workers under 18
ruleCards.text: Workers under 18 need working papers. At 16 and 17 during the school year: 4 hours on school nights, 8 on other days, and after 10 pm only with written consent from a parent and the school. Since May 2025 a first violation can cost up to $10,000.

ruleCards.title: No volunteers
ruleCards.text: A for-profit shop cannot use volunteers. A friend, a cousin or an "intern" who works the counter is an employee: at least $17.00 an hour, on payroll, and covered by workers' compensation from the first hour.

ruleCards.title: Tips are wages
ruleCards.text: Tips are wages for payroll tax: you withhold from them and pay 7.65% on top. Since 2025 workers may deduct up to $25,000 of tips from federal income tax, but only tips that were reported, so unreported cash now costs your staff money.

ruleCards.title: Acting together is protected
ruleCards.text: Two or more workers who talk or act together about pay, schedules or safety are protected by federal law, union or no union, even in a five-person shop. Fire them for it and the labor board orders them rehired with back pay.

ruleCards.title: One day of rest in seven
ruleCards.text: Restaurant employers must give every worker at least 24 hours off in a row each calendar week and name the day in advance (NY Labor Law 161). A worker who agrees to a seventh day does not make it legal.

ruleCards.title: Disability and Paid Family Leave insurance
ruleCards.text: Every NY employer must carry disability and Paid Family Leave insurance. Staff fund family leave through a 0.432% payroll deduction (max $411.91 in 2026). With no policy you pay the claims yourself and commit a misdemeanor.

ruleCards.title: Harassment policy and training
ruleCards.text: Every New York employer, even with 1 worker, needs a written sexual harassment prevention policy and interactive training for every worker every year. The state publishes a free model policy and training.

ruleCards.title: Harassment law covers every employer
ruleCards.text: New York's Human Rights Law covers every employer, whatever its size. Harassment is anything worse than "petty slights", and it includes customers harassing your staff once you know. Act on every complaint and write down what you did.

ruleCards.title: Pay range in every job ad
ruleCards.text: An employer with 4 or more workers must show a pay range in every job ad, even an Instagram post. NYC lets you fix a first violation within 30 days for $0; after that fines run up to $250,000. The state adds up to $3,000.

ruleCards.title: Questions you may not ask
ruleCards.text: In NYC you may not ask applicants about arrests or convictions before a conditional offer, run a credit check, or ask what they earned before. The rules apply from 4 workers, the owner included. Penalties run up to $125,000.

ruleCards.title: Fake reviews
ruleCards.text: Buying reviews, writing your own, or rewarding only good ones breaks the FTC review rule: up to $53,088 per violation. New York's Attorney General once opened a fake yogurt shop to catch sellers of reviews: 19 companies paid over $350,000.

ruleCards.title: Flyers
ruleCards.text: Handing a flyer to a person is legal. Taping it to a pole, a bus shelter or a windshield is not: $75-$150 each the first time, $150-$250 after that, every flyer counted separately, plus removal costs.

ruleCards.title: The office week
ruleCards.text: Offices fill on Tuesday to Thursday. From January to October 2025 only 12.4% of weekday office visits fell on a Friday, and August and December run about a third below 2019. A cafe that lives on office workers has a three-day week.

ruleCards.title: The snow clock
ruleCards.text: When snow stops between 7 AM and 5 PM you have 4 hours to clear your sidewalk; 5 PM to 9 PM, 14 hours; overnight, until 11 AM. A 4-foot path, nothing shoveled into the street. The ticket is $100 per snowfall, and $350 if you ignore the summons.

ruleCards.title: Who pays when someone falls
ruleCards.text: In New York City the building owner, not the city, is liable when someone is hurt on the sidewalk in front (Administrative Code §7-210). Read your lease: most make the store clear the snow and pay the owner back. The average fall claim is $45,000.

ruleCards.title: Sending staff home in a storm
ruleCards.text: Close early for weather and you still owe pay: a restaurant worker who reports for a shift and is sent home is owed three hours at the minimum wage in most cases. Decide before they travel, not after.

ruleCards.title: 18 inches into the street
ruleCards.text: You must keep your sidewalk clean and the gutter too, 18 inches out from the curb, even if someone else dropped the litter. For a business: $50 the first time, $300 the second, $500 the third. Agents come in two fixed hours a day.

ruleCards.title: Sidewalk sheds
ruleCards.text: A shed over your door cuts restaurant and bar transactions by 3.5-9.7% a week. Since 2025 shed permits last 90 days, not a year, and owners pay monthly penalties when no work is done. You may hang a temporary sign on the shed in front of your store.

ruleCards.title: Nobody pays for the dig
ruleCards.text: When the city tears up your street, your sales are your problem. The City's own FAQ: it 'does not have any programs or grants to reimburse a business for lost revenue because of construction.' Ask about the project before you sign a lease.

ruleCards.title: Rain is not in the policy
ruleCards.text: A standard business owner's policy pays for neither flood nor sewer backup. City sewers are built for at most 1.75 inches of rain an hour; on September 29, 2023 parts of Brooklyn got over 3. A water-backup rider costs roughly $50-$250 a year.

ruleCards.title: Winter vestibule
ruleCards.text: A temporary storm enclosure may stand at your door from November 15 to April 15. For most stores it may stick out 18 inches; for an eating place up to 25 square feet, with 5 feet of sidewalk left clear. Inside those limits no building permit is needed.

ruleCards.title: The card stays in the window
ruleCards.text: The grade card must hang where people walking by can see it. No card: $500, or $1,000 if you skip the hearing. Removing, hiding or faking it: $1,000, or $2,000. Every card has a serial number.

ruleCards.title: Hand sinks
ruleCards.text: Every hand sink needs hot and cold water, soap and paper towels, and must stay clear. A dead hand sink is 10 points; at the worst level it is 28 points, a C by itself, and the inspector can close you until it works.

ruleCards.title: No bare hands
ruleCards.text: Food that is ready to eat may not be touched with bare hands: use tongs, tissue or gloves for every pastry and garnish. It is a public health hazard: $250 to $600 per citation.

ruleCards.title: Dogs
ruleCards.text: Pet dogs may not come inside a food shop: $200-$350 and a critical violation. Service dogs must be allowed wherever customers go, tag or no tag. Pets may sit at outdoor tables only if you opt in and post the sign.

ruleCards.title: Let the inspector in
ruleCards.text: Refusing or delaying a health inspection costs $1,000, and the inspection still happens. One owner who refused an inspection as a protest had his restaurant closed by the Health Department.

ruleCards.title: Signs on the wall
ruleCards.text: Restaurants must post the choking first aid poster, the CPR kit notice, hand-wash signs, no smoking signs and the Healthy Eating poster. The city gives them away free through 311. A missing one costs about $200.

ruleCards.title: Allergy notice
ruleCards.text: New York requires an allergy notice on every menu, online menus too, and an allergy poster where staff can see it, in their languages. From January 2027 the city writes $100 summonses; state law allows up to $125.

ruleCards.title: Extinguisher tags
ruleCards.text: Extinguishers need a yearly service by an FDNY-certified company and a quick check every month, dated and initialed on the tag. A missing or expired tag: $600, or $300 if you fix it and show proof at the hearing.

ruleCards.title: Keep the exit clear
ruleCards.text: Exit doors and the path to them must stay clear at all times. Boxes in the back corridor cost $950, or $475 if cleared before the hearing; a second ticket is $2,375.

ruleCards.title: How many people fit
ruleCards.text: A room that gathers 75 or more people needs a Place of Assembly certificate. Overcrowding a small cafe costs $950, then $2,375, and fire officers can clear the room in the middle of your event.

ruleCards.title: Candles
ruleCards.text: Candles on restaurant tables need an FDNY open flame permit: $210 a year. Without it: $700, or $350 if you get the permit before the hearing.

ruleCards.title: Your sidewalk, your broom
ruleCards.text: You must sweep your sidewalk and 18 inches into the street. Each is a separate ticket of $100 to $300. Sanitation agents may ticket a business for this only during two set one-hour windows a day.

ruleCards.title: 42 decibels
ruleCards.text: Music from a business may not exceed 42 decibels inside a neighbor's home. First violation $2,000, then $4,000, then $6,000. A first offender who fixes it and files a noise consultant's report can have the $2,000 cut to $0.

ruleCards.title: Card fees must be posted
ruleCards.text: You may add a credit card surcharge only if the full card price is posted and the fee is no more than your processing cost. A surprise fee at the register: up to $500 per violation. Debit cards cannot be surcharged.

ruleCards.title: Music needs a license
ruleCards.text: Music in a shop is a public performance, and a personal streaming account is not a license. Copyright law allows $750 to $30,000 per song; restaurant judgments have averaged about $3,600 a song.

ruleCards.title: Free posters, real duty
ruleCards.text: NYC employers must post the city's 'Your Rights at Work' poster and hand a copy to every worker on day one. First miss: 30 days to fix. After that: $500. Official posters are free; mailers asking $92.58 for one are a scam.

ruleCards.title: No smoking, no vaping
ruleCards.text: No smoking or vaping inside or at your outdoor tables. Post the signs and keep a written policy. Fines for the owner: $200-$400 the first time, $500-$1,000 the second, $1,000-$2,000 the third.

ruleCards.title: CBD in drinks
ruleCards.text: New York City's Health Department does not allow CBD added to food or drinks in restaurants and cafes: inspectors embargo the product, and fines have run $200 to $650.

ruleCards.title: Payroll taxes are held in trust
ruleCards.text: Taxes withheld from pay in one month are due at the IRS by the 15th of the next. Late deposits cost 2% to 15%. Use the money for rent and the IRS can bill 100% of the withheld tax to you personally (Trust Fund Recovery Penalty).

ruleCards.title: Fees on top of menu prices
ruleCards.text: A New York City restaurant may not add a surcharge to its listed prices: no "living wage fee", no "admin charge". A real service charge, such as a tip for parties of eight or more, must be disclosed before the customer orders.

ruleCards.title: No water, no service
ruleCards.text: A food business needs hot and cold running water every open minute. Without it the Health Department treats the shop as a public health hazard and can close it on the spot.

ruleCards.title: Plastic straws on request
ruleCards.text: Plastic straws only when a customer asks, free, no questions. Self-serve stations need a sign. Fines $100-$400 per violation.

benchmarks.note: D00 correction: the source reports nationwide limited-service median income BEFORE tax of 4.0%, not after-tax net margin. The existing netMarginPct field is a legacy proxy requiring a schema/label correction. COGS 28%, labor 35% and rent 10% remain independent planning assumptions, not source medians. In particular 65% minus 28% is 37%, not 35%; separate sample medians should not be treated as additive components. No numeric benchmark is re-estimated here.

suppliers.what: Wholesale roasted beans in 5 lb bags, usually with barista training and equipment service included
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask the cafes you like who roasts for them, then visit two or three roasters for a cupping. Ask each for the price list, the minimum, the roast day and what happens to the price when the market moves.
suppliers.examples: Partners Coffee, Joe Coffee Company, Brooklyn Roasting Company, Variety Coffee Roasters, Devocion, Counter Culture Coffee
suppliers.note: Correction of the existing entry: terms added. Seen through search: Joe Coffee 5 lb Waverly blend $80 on Faire ($16.00 per lb); Atomic $17.20 per lb (research notes); Dilworth $11.75 and $15.25 per lb; Klatch minimum 15 lb an order; Kean 40 lb a month in 5 lb bags; Methodical no minimum; a trade guide: cafes order 5-25 lb a week at $10-$15 per lb, tiers $12 and $11, terms net 15-30; a green coffee importer: net 30 after three orders, 1.5% a month on late balances; a roaster's own case study on warehouse beans one to three months old. Roaster names are well-known examples, not endorsements.

suppliers.what: Whole milk by the gallon, half-and-half and cream, delivered two to six mornings a week
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask the neighboring cafes which dairy truck already stops on your block: a route that passes your door is cheaper than one that detours. Ask who owns the crates and what an unreturned crate costs.
suppliers.examples: Dairy routes run by regional processors and by specialty distributors such as Baldor or Dairyland (The Chefs' Warehouse); Restaurant Depot for emergencies
suppliers.note: Correction of the existing entry: terms added. Seen through search: Baldor's help center gives order minimums of $200, $350 or $500 for accounts served from the Bronx warehouse depending on distance and no delivery fee for business accounts; Toast's invoice data gives $5.28 a gallon for whole milk (year not stated). Delivery hours and crate practice are trade knowledge, not a published tariff.

suppliers.what: Croissants, muffins, cookies and bread baked overnight by a licensed wholesale bakery and delivered before opening
suppliers.whereToFind: Wholesale programs of local bakeries: ask for the wholesale menu, the minimum, the order deadline and the days they do not bake. Ask whether they credit anything for damaged goods; nobody credits unsold ones.
suppliers.examples: Balthazar Bakery, Bien Cuit, Ceci-Cela, Colson Patisserie, Pain d'Avignon, Orwashers, Amy's Bread

suppliers.what: Espresso machine, grinders, refrigeration, sinks, dishwasher, shelving
suppliers.whereToFind: Online restaurant supply stores for list prices; the restaurant supply shops on the Bowery in Manhattan to see things in person; your roaster for the espresso machine, often with a service contract.
suppliers.examples: WebstaurantStore, KaTom, Visions Espresso, Restaurant Depot, Bowery restaurant supply shops
suppliers.note: Prices in this pack were seen at WebstaurantStore and Visions Espresso on November 14, 2026. Names are well-known examples from general knowledge of the New York market, not endorsements and not checked in this session unless a link is given; compare at least three quotes.

suppliers.what: Second-hand machines, fridges and furniture at roughly half the new price
suppliers.whereToFind: Cafes that are closing (ask brokers and landlords), restaurant equipment auctions, used dealers on the Bowery, Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist. Have a technician test an espresso machine before you pay.
suppliers.examples: Restaurant auction houses, used equipment dealers on the Bowery, the previous tenant of your space
suppliers.note: The "half price" figure is my rough estimate. The research notes' cheapest opening budget assumes part of the previous cafe's equipment is kept. Names are well-known examples from general knowledge of the New York market, not endorsements and not checked in this session unless a link is given; compare at least three quotes.

suppliers.what: Cups, lids, sleeves, bags, wooden stirrers, napkins, straws kept for those who ask
